lecture.title: Data Management Evolution, DBS Components & Classical Data Models
objectives: Distinguish Data, Database (DB), Database Management System (DBMS), and Database System (DBS)
Compare the 3 stages of data management technology development: Manual Management, File System, and DBS
Contrast Hierarchical, Network, and Relational database models and trace SQL standardization history
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Core Concepts: Data, DB, DBMS, and DBS
- **Data**: Facts or statistics represented as discrete **digital data** (symbols, characters, numerals) or continuous **analog data** (audio, video, images). Raw data is meaningless until processed into **information**.
- **Database (DB)**: A **permanent**, **organized**, and **sharable** collection of structured data stored in a computer according to a data model with minimal redundancy and high independence.
- **Database Management System (DBMS)**: System software between the user/application and OS that manages the DB. Its 5 core functions are:
  1. **Data Definition (DDL)** — defining tables, views, indexes, and schemas.
  2. **Data Manipulation (DML)** — querying, inserting, deleting, and updating data.
  3. **Database Operation Management** — ensuring security, integrity checks, concurrency control, and fault recovery.
  4. **Interfaces & Tools** — APIs for developers and O&M tools for DBAs.
  5. **Creation & Maintenance** — initial data conversion, dump/restore, and performance monitoring.
- **Database System (DBS)**: The complete operational ecosystem. Per Huawei's official definition (p. 9), **a DBS consists of three core parts**:
  1. **Database (DB)** — stores data.
  2. **DBMS** — manages the database.
  3. **Database Applications** — supplement the DBMS to provide intuitive user-facing data processing (along with DBAs and users).
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Database System (DBS) Component Stack Diagram (Official Reference: p. 9)](./assets/images/p3_h1s1_dbs_components.png)
*Figure: Database System (DBS) Component Stack Diagram (Official Reference: p. 9)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Three Stages of Data Management Technology Development

| Dimension | 1. Manual Management (Mid-1950s) | 2. File System (Late 1950s – Mid-1960s) | 3. DBS Stage (Late 1960s – Present) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Application** | Scientific computing | Scientific computing & management | Large-scale & distributed data management |
| **Hardware** | Paper tapes, punch cards (no direct access storage) | Magnetic tapes, disks, magnetic drums | Large-capacity disks, arrays, on-demand expansion |
| **Software / Manager** | None (managed by User/Program) | File System | **DBMS / DBS** |
| **Data Sharing** | No sharing; high redundancy | Poor sharing; high redundancy | **Good sharing; low redundancy** |
| **Data Independence** | Poor (program-bound) | Good physical independence; poor logical independence | **High physical & good logical independence** |
| **Data Structuring** | Unstructured | Structured inside a record; unstructured as a whole | **Unified data model & overall structuring** |
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Three Stages of Data Management Development (Official Reference: p. 10)](./assets/images/p3_h1s1_data_mgmt_stages.png)
*Figure: Three Stages of Data Management Development (Official Reference: p. 10)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. Classical Database Models & SQL Evolution
- **Hierarchical Model (1960s, e.g., IBM IMS, DNS, LDAP, Linux/Windows FS)**: Tree structure where only the **root node** has no parent, and every other node has **exactly one parent node** (1:N).
- **Network Model**: Graph structure allowing **more than one node to have no parent**, and a node can have **more than one parent** (M:N).
- **Relational Model (1969/1970, E.F. Codd)**: Uses rigorous two-dimensional tables (**Relations**) composed of rows (**Tuples**), columns (**Attributes**), and primary identifiers (**Keys / Codes**). Relationships must be normalized so every attribute is an indivisible atomic data item.
- **SQL Standardization Milestones**:
  - **SQL-86 (1986)**: First ANSI SQL standard.
  - **SQL-89 (1989)**: Added integrity constraints.
  - **SQL-92 / SQL2 (1992)**: Introduced standard classification concepts.
  - **SQL:1999 / SQL3 (1999)**: Major revision adding object-oriented features, regular expressions, triggers, and recursive queries.
  - **SQL:2003**: XML & Window functions; **SQL:2008**: `TRUNCATE`; **SQL:2011**: Temporal/time-series; **SQL:2016**: JSON.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Hierarchical (Tree), Network (Graph), and Relational Models (Official Reference: p. 18)](./assets/images/p3_h1s1_database_models.png)
*Figure: Hierarchical (Tree), Network (Graph), and Relational Models (Official Reference: p. 18)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: A Database System (DBS) consists of three parts: Database (DB), DBMS, and Database Application (storage medium is hardware, NOT one of the three logical DBS components in Ch.01 Quiz Q1).
Data management evolved through exactly three stages: Manual Management, File System, and Database System (DBS).
In the relational model, each cell must be an indivisible data item; in the hierarchical model, every non-root node has only one parent; in the network model, a node can have multiple parents.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.01 Quiz Q1): 'Which of the following is NOT a component of a database system?' -> D. Database storage medium! The three components are Database, DBMS, and Database application.

EXAM TRAP (Ch.01 Quiz Q3): 'Which phases are involved in the development of data management technologies?' -> A. Manual management, B. File system, C. DBS (ABC). 'AI management' (D) is NOT one of the three historical stages!

lecture.title: Transactions (ACID), NoSQL vs NewSQL & Database Deployment Architectures
objectives: Trace the 5 transaction execution states and explain the 4 ACID properties
Compare Relational Databases, NoSQL (CAP Theorem), and NewSQL
Contrast Single-Node, Master/Backup, Master/Slave, Multi-Master, Shared-Disk, Sharding, Shared-Nothing MPP, and OLTP vs OLAP
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Database Transactions & ACID Properties
A **transaction** is an indivisible logical unit of work used for database recovery and concurrency control.
- **5 Transaction States (p. 21)**:
  1. **Active**: Initial state while statements are executing.
  2. **Partially committed**: Immediately after the final statement executes, before disk flush completes.
  3. **Failed**: Normal execution can no longer proceed.
  4. **Aborted**: Transaction is rolled back and database is restored to its pre-transaction state.
  5. **Committed**: All operations succeeded and changes are permanently stored.
- **ACID Properties (p. 22)**:
  - **Atomicity (A)**: Either all operations in the transaction succeed or none do (all-or-nothing rollback on failure).
  - **Consistency (C)**: A transaction transitions the database from one valid/consistent state to another (e.g., total money across accounts before and after transfer remains invariant).
  - **Isolation (I)**: Concurrent transactions execute independently without interfering with each other or exposing uncommitted intermediate states.
  - **Durability (D)**: Once committed, changes are permanent and survive power loss or system crashes (implemented via **WAL — Write-Ahead Logging**).
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Database Transaction Execution State Machine (Active, Committed, Failed, End) (Official Reference: p. 20)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_tx_states.png)
*Figure: Database Transaction Execution State Machine (Active, Committed, Failed, End) (Official Reference: p. 20)*

![ACID Isolation Concurrent Transactions (T1 and T2) (Official Reference: p. 22)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_acid_isolation.png)
*Figure: ACID Isolation Concurrent Transactions (T1 and T2) (Official Reference: p. 22)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. NoSQL (CAP Theory) vs. NewSQL
- **NoSQL ("Not Only SQL")**: Designed for ultra-large-scale concurrent access without fixed schemas:
  1. **Key-Value**: Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB.
  2. **Document (JSON)**: MongoDB, CouchDB, Couchbase.
  3. **Search Engine**: Elasticsearch, Solr, Splunk.
  4. **Wide-Column / Distributed**: HBase, Cassandra.
- **CAP Theorem**: A distributed system can satisfy at most **two** of **Consistency (C)**, **Availability (A)**, and **Partition Tolerance (P)**. Because network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems (**P is mandatory**), distributed NoSQL systems must balance between **CP** (e.g., HBase, MongoDB, Redis) and **AP** (e.g., Cassandra, Dynamo, CouchDB), whereas traditional single-site RDBMSs are **CA**.
- **NewSQL (`SQL + NoSQL = NewSQL`)**: Combines the horizontal scalability of NoSQL with the relational model, SQL interface, and ACID transactions of RDBMS (e.g., Google Spanner, VoltDB, GaussDB).

---

### 3. Evolution of Relational Database Architectures & OLTP vs. OLAP

| Architecture | Key Characteristics | Pros & Bottlenecks |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Single-Node / Standalone** | App & DB separated on standalone server | Easy O&M; limited to vertical **Scale-Up**, suffers from SPOF. |
| **Master/Backup** | Master does R/W; Backup is idle until failover | Improves fault tolerance; wastes standby resources; single-node perf limit. |
| **Master/Slave** | Master handles Writes; Slaves handle Reads | Read/write isolation scales reads; replication lag causes temporary inconsistency. |
| **Multi-Master** | Active-active bidirectional R/W | High resource utilization; complex bidirectional sync and conflict resolution. |
| **Shared-Disk** | Multiple compute nodes share SAN/FC storage (e.g., Oracle RAC) | High availability; storage I/O bus bandwidth becomes bottleneck. |
| **Shared-Nothing / MPP** | Each node has independent CPU, RAM, and disk; horizontal **Sharding** | Near-linear **Scale-Out**, no shared bottleneck (e.g., GaussDB, DB2 DPF). |

- **OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)** vs. **OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)**:
  - **OLTP**: Routine short transactions (insert/update/delete), read/write, dozens of rows via index/hash, 100 MB–GB scale, measured by **transaction throughput (tpmC)** and memory efficiency.
  - **OLAP**: Decision support & data warehousing, complex multi-dimensional aggregation queries, mostly reads, millions of rows via full/partition scans, 100 GB–TB+ scale, measured by **disk I/O bandwidth and query response time**.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Relational Database Deployment Architecture Taxonomy (Official Reference: p. 31)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_arch_evolution.png)
*Figure: Relational Database Deployment Architecture Taxonomy (Official Reference: p. 31)*

![Single Node vs Standalone Database Deployment (Official Reference: p. 32)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_single_node.png)
*Figure: Single Node vs Standalone Database Deployment (Official Reference: p. 32)*

![Grouping Deployment: Master/Backup Topology (Official Reference: p. 33)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_master_backup.png)

![Grouping Deployment: Master/Slave (Read/Write Split) Topology (Official Reference: p. 34)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_master_slave.png)
*Figure: Grouping Deployment: Master/Slave (Read/Write Split) Topology (Official Reference: p. 34)*

![Grouping Deployment: Multi-Master Topology (Official Reference: p. 35)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_multi_master.png)
*Figure: Grouping Deployment: Multi-Master Topology (Official Reference: p. 35)*

![Shared Disk Multi-Master Cluster Topology (Official Reference: p. 36)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_shared_disk.png)
*Figure: Shared Disk Multi-Master Cluster Topology (Official Reference: p. 36)*

![Horizontal vs Vertical Database Sharding Diagram (Official Reference: p. 37)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_sharding_split.png)
*Figure: Horizontal vs Vertical Database Sharding Diagram (Official Reference: p. 37)*

![Shared-Nothing Distributed Architecture (Official Reference: p. 38)](./assets/images/p3_h1s2_shared_nothing.png)

*Figure: Massively Parallel Processing (MPP) Execution Topology (Official Reference: p. 39)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: In ACID, 'I' stands for Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), NOT Availability!
CAP Theorem states a distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency (C), Availability (A), and Partition Tolerance (P).
Shared-Nothing (MPP) gives each node independent CPU, memory, and disk, enabling near-linear horizontal scale-out.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.01 Quiz Q2): Option C claims 'I refers to availability, whereby the database system must provide the highest availability possible'. That is INCORRECT! 'I' stands for Isolation.
EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse Master/Backup (standby does NOT provide read services during normal operation) with Master/Slave (slave provides read services via read/write splitting).

quiz_questions.question: (Official Ch.01 Quiz Q2) Which of the following statements about the ACID feature of database transactions is INCORRECT?
options: A. A indicates atomicity, whereby operations in a transaction are either all successful or all failed.
B. C refers to consistency, whereby the system status can only be the status before the transaction or after the transaction is successful. No inconsistent intermediate status can occur.

C. I refers to availability, whereby the database system must provide the highest availability possible for transaction execution in order to ensure as many successfully executed transactions as possible.
D. D refers to durability, whereby the status of a successful transaction can be maintained, even if the machine is powered off.
quiz_questions.explanation: In ACID, 'I' stands for Isolation (transactions are isolated from each other and do not interfere when executed concurrently), NOT Availability.

quiz_questions.question: In which multi-node database architecture does each processing unit have its own independent CPU, memory, and hard disk without sharing hardware resources?
quiz_questions.explanation: In Shared-Nothing (and MPP) architecture, each node has its own private CPU, memory, and disk, communicating via network protocols for horizontal scale-out.

quiz_questions.question: According to the CAP theory for distributed systems, a distributed database can simultaneously satisfy Consistency (C), Availability (A), and Partition Tolerance (P) at all times.
quiz_questions.explanation: False. CAP theory states that a distributed system can satisfy at most TWO of Consistency (C), Availability (A), and Partition Tolerance (P) at the same time.

lecture.title: openGauss Positioning, Evolution & Differences from PostgreSQL
objectives: Trace openGauss's evolution from internal incubation (2001) to open-source release (June 30, 2020) under Mulan PSL v2
Explain the 4 core value pillars of openGauss: High Performance, High Availability, High Security, and Easy O&M
Contrast openGauss and PostgreSQL across process/thread model, concurrency control, checkpoints, NUMA, and storage engines
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. openGauss Positioning, License & Evolution Timeline
**openGauss** is an enterprise-grade, multi-core-optimized open-source relational database developed by Huawei with global partners.
- **Open-Source License**: Released under **Mulan Permissive Software License v2 (Mulan PSL v2)** — allowing code to be freely modified, used, and referenced commercially.
- **4 Milestones in openGauss History (p. 44)**:
  1. **2001–2011 (Internal Incubation)**: Enterprise in-memory database used across Huawei telecom carrier products.
  2. **2011–2019 (Productization & Joint Innovation)**: Commercialized on HUAWEI CLOUD DWS and major banks; **GaussDB globally released on May 15, 2019**; openGauss open-source announced on **September 19, 2019**.
  3. **June 30, 2020 (Official Open Source)**: Source code officially opened at `https://gitee.com/opengauss`.
  4. **2021–Future (Ecosystem Building)**: Community governance via Technical Committee (**TC**), **SIGs** (SQL Engine, Storage Engine, Connectors, Docs, Infra, Security), **Maintainers**, **Committers**, and **Contributors**.

---

### 2. Core Value Pillars of openGauss (p. 46)
1. **High Performance**: **1.5 million tpmC** on 2-socket Kunpeng 920 (128 cores); NUMA-aware data structures; **SQL-Bypass** intelligent fast path; in-memory **MOT** engine.
2. **High Availability (HA)**: Hitless primary/standby switchover and Parallel Redo **Ultimate RTO < 10s**.
3. **High Security**: End-to-end protection including **Fully-Encrypted Equality Query** (TEE/secGear), Dynamic Data Masking, RBAC, RLS, Unified Auditing, and TDE.
4. **Easy O&M**: Built-in **DBMind AI** (parameter tuning, slow SQL diagnosis, index recommendation, workload time prediction) and WDR snapshots.

---

### 3. Architectural Comparison: openGauss vs. PostgreSQL (pp. 48–49)

| Differentiation Dimension | openGauss | PostgreSQL |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Execution Model** | **Single-process multi-threaded (`gaussdb`)** with thread pool | **Multi-process (`postgres`)** — one process per client connection |
| **Transaction ID & Concurrency** | **64-bit Transaction ID (XID)** + **CSN (Commit Sequence Number)**; eliminates XID wraparound & resolves the "five big locks" bottleneck | 32-bit XID wraparound causes periodic VACUUM FREEZE performance drops; "five big locks" limit multi-core scaling |
| **Logs & Checkpoints** | **Incremental checkpoint**, keeping performance fluctuation **< 5%** | **Full checkpoint**, causing short-term performance fluctuation **> 15%** |
| **Kunpeng NUMA Scaling** | NUMA data structure reconstruction, cache-line padding, ARMv8.1 native `casal` spin-lock (**1.5M tpmC** on 2-socket Kunpeng) | Weak NUMA multi-core capability (**< 600,000 tpmC** on dual-socket server) |
| **Storage Engines** | **Multi-engine**: Row-store (Astore/Ustore in-place update), Column-store, and **MOT (Memory-Optimized Table)** | **Row-store only** (append-only MVCC) |
| **Optimizer & SQL** | CBO + **ABO (AI-Based Optimizer)**; SQL92/99/2003/2011 + enterprise extensions | Standard CBO; average performance in complex enterprise queries |
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Thread Pool Architecture vs PostgreSQL Multi-Process Architecture (Official Reference: p. 48)](./assets/images/p3_h1s3_opengauss_vs_pg.png)
*Figure: openGauss Thread Pool Architecture vs PostgreSQL Multi-Process Architecture (Official Reference: p. 48)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: openGauss uses a single-process multi-threaded architecture (`gaussdb`), whereas PostgreSQL uses a multi-process architecture.

openGauss uses 64-bit transaction IDs with Commit Sequence Numbers (CSNs) and incremental checkpoints (< 5% fluctuation), solving PostgreSQL's 32-bit XID wraparound and full checkpoint (> 15% fluctuation) bottlenecks.
openGauss officially went open source on June 30, 2020 under the Mulan PSL v2 license.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: PostgreSQL supports only row-store natively, whereas openGauss supports Row-store, Column-store, and Memory-Optimized Table (MOT) engines.
EXAM TRAP: On 2-socket Kunpeng 920 (128 cores), openGauss achieves 1.5 million tpmC (1.5x higher than x86 alternatives), with RTO < 10s.

lecture.title: openGauss Technical Specifications, APIs (`ODBC`/`JDBC`) & SQL Hints
objectives: Identify the 4 categories of execution engine plan nodes (Scan, Control, Materialize, Join)
Memorize official openGauss technical specifications (32 TB table size, 1 GB row/field, 10,000 connections, partition limits)
Configure standard SQL, ODBC 3.5, JDBC 4.0 (JDK 1.8), libpq/ECPG APIs, WAL/Checkpoint transaction durability, and SQL Plan Hints
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Query Optimization, Execution Engine & Storage Engine (pp. 52–54)
- **Physical Query Optimization Pipeline**:
  `Table/Column Statistics (Unique + MCV)` -> `Row Estimation (baserel/joinrel/agg)` -> `Cost Estimation` -> `Access Path Generation (Dynamic Programming / Genetic Algorithm)` -> `PlanTree Generation`.
- **4 Categories of Execution Engine Plan Nodes (pp. 53–54)**:
  1. **Scan plan nodes** (Leaf nodes, input data + expression filtering): `SeqScan`, `IndexScan`, `SubQueryScan`.
  2. **Control plan nodes** (Flow control): `Limit`, `RecursiveUnion`, `Union`.
  3. **Materialize plan nodes** (Cache lower-layer data; return only after all data is scanned): `Agg`, `Sort`.
  4. **Join plan nodes** (Multiple inputs): `MergeJoin`, `SortJoin` / `NestLoop`, `HashJoin`.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Execution Engine Pipeline (Scan, Plan, Materialization, Join) (Official Reference: p. 53)](./assets/images/p3_h1s4_execution_engine.png)
*Figure: openGauss Execution Engine Pipeline (Scan, Plan, Materialization, Join) (Official Reference: p. 53)*

![openGauss Storage Engine Layered Stack (Official Reference: p. 54)](./assets/images/p3_h1s4_storage_engine.png)
*Figure: openGauss Storage Engine Layered Stack (Official Reference: p. 54)*

![Kunpeng Multi-Core CPU Architecture and Dual-Socket Performance (Official Reference: p. 55)](./assets/images/p3_h1s4_kunpeng_numa_perf.png)
*Figure: Kunpeng Multi-Core CPU Architecture and Dual-Socket Performance (Official Reference: p. 55)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Official openGauss Technical Specifications (p. 57)

| Technical Specification Item | Official Maximum Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Database capacity** | Varies depending on the OS and hardware |
| **Maximum size of a single table** | **32 TB** |
| **Maximum size of data in a single row / single field** | **1 GB** (Row) / **1 GB** (Field) |
| **Maximum number of records in each table** | **2^{48}** |
| **Number of columns in a single table** | **250 to 1,600** (varies with field type) |
| **Number of indexes / constraints on a single table** | **Unlimited** |
| **Maximum columns in a composite index** | **32** (up to 16 recommended in DDL guide) |
| **Maximum concurrent connections** | **10,000** |
| **Maximum partitions in a partitioned table** | **32,768 (Range partitioning)** / **64 (Hash or List partitioning)** |
| **Size of each partition / records per partition** | **32 TB** / **2^{55} records** |

---

### 3. Standard APIs, Transaction WAL Mechanism & SQL Hints (pp. 59–66)
- **Standard SQL**: Supports SQL-92, SQL-99, **SQL:2003** standard, and core/optional features of **SQL:2011**.
- **ODBC 3.5**: Uses `unixODBC-2.3.0` or `iODBC` on Linux/UNIX, or native Windows ODBC Driver Manager. *(Note: Current open-source ODBC driver may be incompatible with `tinyint`, `smalldatetime`, and `nvarchar2`.)*
- **JDBC 4.0**: Requires **JDK 1.8** for compilation; supports third-party logging frameworks; **does NOT support JDBC-ODBC bridging**.
- **PostgreSQL Client APIs**: Compatible with **libpq** (C API foundation) and **ECPG** (Embedded SQL in C).
- **Transaction Mechanism (p. 62–63)**:
  - Default transaction isolation level is **`READ COMMITTED`** (prevents dirty reads).
  - Durability is guaranteed by **WAL (Write-Ahead Logging)** — redo logs are flushed to disk upon commit before data pages, while **Checkpoints** flush dirty buffers from the dirty buffer queue to data files.
- **SQL Plan Hints (`/*+ ... */`)**: Override the optimizer's execution plan by specifying join order, join method (`HashJoin`, `MergeJoin`, `NestLoop`), scan method (`IndexScan`, `SeqScan`), stream mode, or row estimates.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Fully-Encrypted Database Equality Query (Client Driver to TEE) (Official Reference: p. 56)](./assets/images/p3_h1s4_fully_encrypted_tee.png)
*Figure: openGauss Fully-Encrypted Database Equality Query (Client Driver to TEE) (Official Reference: p. 56)*

![Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) Redo Buffer and Checkpoint Disk Flush Flow (Official Reference: p. 63)](./assets/images/p3_h1s4_wal_redo_mechanism.png)
*Figure: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) Redo Buffer and Checkpoint Disk Flush Flow (Official Reference: p. 63)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: openGauss supports up to 32 TB per table, 1 GB per row/field, 10,000 concurrent connections, 32,768 range partitions, and 64 hash/list partitions.
The default transaction isolation level in openGauss is READ COMMITTED, and durability is enforced via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL).
openGauss supports ODBC 3.5, JDBC 4.0 (requires JDK 1.8, no JDBC-ODBC bridge), libpq, and ECPG.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Range partitioning supports up to 32,768 partitions per table, whereas Hash and List partitioning support up to 64 partitions (Ch.01 p. 57).
EXAM TRAP: Materialize plan nodes (such as Agg and Sort) return data ONLY after all lower-layer data has been scanned and cached.

lecture.title: Deployment Modes, Hardware/OS Prerequisites & XML Configuration
objectives: Compare the 3 official openGauss deployment modes: Standalone, Primary/Standby, and One Primary + Multiple Standbys
Verify hardware (RAM, CPU, Disk, NIC MTU) and software/OS prerequisites (openEuler, Python 3.7, libaio-devel)
Configure OS settings prior to installation: SELinux, firewalld, RemoveIPC=no, locale/timezone, NIC MTU, root SSH, and `dbgrp`/`omm`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Three Official openGauss Deployment Modes (pp. 77–81, Ch.03 Quiz Q1!)

| Deployment Mode | Data Copies | HA / RPO / RTO | Key Characteristics & Target Scenario |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Standalone (Single-node)** | **1 copy** | No HA; RTO & RPO uncontrollable | Single instance; lost instance data can only be restored from physical backup. For **trial use, learning, and sandbox testing** (not production). |
| **2. Primary/Standby (1 Primary + 1 Standby)** | **2 copies** | **RPO = 0**, Instance fault **RTO < 10s** | Primary supports Read/Write; Standby receives/replays WAL logs and supports **Read-only**. Protects against instance failure. |
| **3. One Primary + Multiple Standbys (Quorum)** | **2 to 4 copies** (typically 1P + 2S = **3 copies**; up to 8 standbys in v2.0+) | **RPO = 0**, Instance fault **RTO < 10s**, **99.99% reliability** | Quorum replication synchronizes data to at least one standby node for max performance. Primary and standby nodes **cannot** be on the same physical machine. |

> **CRITICAL EXAM NOTE (Ch.03 Quiz Q1)**: openGauss supports **Single-node**, **One primary + one standby**, and **One primary + multiple standbys**. It **DOES NOT** support "Dual primary nodes" deployment!
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Standalone Deployment Architecture (Official Reference: p. 78)](./assets/images/p3_h2s1_standalone_deploy.png)
*Figure: openGauss Standalone Deployment Architecture (Official Reference: p. 78)*

![openGauss Primary/Standby Deployment Topology (Official Reference: p. 79)](./assets/images/p3_h2s1_primary_standby.png)
*Figure: openGauss Primary/Standby Deployment Topology (Official Reference: p. 79)*

![openGauss One Primary and Multiple Standbys Topology (Official Reference: p. 80)](./assets/images/p3_h2s1_one_primary_multi_standby.png)
*Figure: openGauss One Primary and Multiple Standbys Topology (Official Reference: p. 80)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Hardware & Software Requirements (pp. 84–85)
- **Memory**: **>= 32 GB** for function debugging; **>= 128 GB** for commercial/performance testing; **4 GB min (8 GB recommended)** for individual developers.
- **CPU**: At least one 8-core 2.0 GHz CPU (debugging) or 16-core 2.0 GHz CPU (commercial); 2 cores min (4 cores recommended) for individual developers. Supports **Kunpeng (ARM64)** and **x86_64**.
- **Disk**: At least **1 GB** for application installation, **>= 300 MB** per host for data, and **> 70% free space** reserved for data storage. Recommended: **RAID 1 for system disk**, **4 groups of RAID 5 for data disks**, Disk Cache Policy = **Disabled**.
- **Network**: >= 300 Mbit/s Ethernet (bond 2 NICs recommended). Recommended **MTU**: **1500 for x86**, **8192 for ARM (Kunpeng)**.
- **OS & Software Dependencies**:
  - **OS**: Arm (`openEuler 20.03/22.03 LTS`, `KylinOS`); x86 (`openEuler 20.03/22.03 LTS`, `CentOS 7.6`).
  - **File system**: Remaining inodes **> 1.5 billion**.
  - **Python**: **Python 3.7.x** on openEuler/KylinOS; **Python 3.6.x** on CentOS 7.6.
  - **Packages**: `bzip2`, `libaio-devel` (0.3.109-13), `readline-devel` (7.0-13), `expect`.

---

### 3. Mandatory OS Configuration Changes & User Planning (pp. 86–91)
1. **Disable SELinux & Firewall**: Set `SELINUX=disabled` in `/etc/selinux/config`, reboot, and run `systemctl disable firewalld.service && systemctl stop firewalld.service`.
2. **Locale & Timezone**: Add `export LANG=en_US.UTF-8` to `/etc/profile`; copy `/usr/share/zoneinfo/Locale/Timezone` to `/etc/localtime` and sync time with `date -s`. Optional: `swapoff -a` to prevent buffer eviction.
3. **Disable `RemoveIPC` (Critical on openEuler!)**: Set `RemoveIPC=no` in **both** `/etc/systemd/logind.conf` and `/usr/lib/systemd/system/systemd-logind.service`, then run `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart systemd-logind`.
4. **Enable Root SSH & Disable Banner**: In `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, set `PermitRootLogin yes` and comment out `#Banner XXXX` (welcome banners interfere with remote installation scripts).
5. **User & Group (`dbgrp` and `omm`)**: Create group `dbgrp` (`-G dbgrp`) and OS user `omm` (`-U omm`). During `gs_install`, a database superuser `omm` with the same name is created.
key_takeaways: openGauss deployment modes are Single-node, One primary + one standby, and One primary + multiple standbys (up to 8 standbys; typically 1 primary + 2 standbys for 99.99% availability). Dual-primary is NOT supported.
On openEuler (ARM64), set RemoveIPC=no in both logind.conf and systemd-logind.service, disable SELinux and firewalld, comment out SSH Banner, and set NIC MTU to 8192 (1500 on x86).
System disk should use RAID 1, data disks should use 4 groups of RAID 5 with Disk Cache Policy Disabled, and remaining inodes should exceed 1.5 billion.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.03 Quiz Q1): 'Which of the following are the openGauss deployment modes?' -> A. Single-node, B. One primary and one standby, C. One primary and multiple standbys (ABC). D. Dual primary nodes is FALSE!
EXAM TRAP: Why comment out `Banner` in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`? Because welcome banner text interferes with automated remote SSH operations during `gs_preinstall` and `gs_install`!

lecture.title: Installing (`install.sh` / `gs_preinstall` / `gs_install`), Starting/Stopping & Uninstalling openGauss
objectives: Verify all 4 official prerequisites for single-node openGauss installation (Ch.02 Quiz Q3)
Execute both Simplified Single-Node Installation (`sh install.sh -w`) and Standard Enterprise XML Installation (`gs_preinstall` + `gs_install`)
Start and stop openGauss (`gs_om -t start/stop`) and cleanly uninstall (`gs_uninstall --delete-data` + `gs_postuninstall`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Single-Node Installation Prerequisites & Procedure (pp. 92–93, Ch.02 Quiz Q3!)
Before installing openGauss on a single node, **four prerequisites** must be met (exact **Ch.02 Quiz Q3: ABCD**):
1. **Users & OS/Network**: A user group and a common user have been created, and all server OSs and networks are functioning properly.
2. **Directory Permissions**: Common users must have **read, write, and execute (`rwx`)** permissions on the database package decompression directory and installation directory, and the **installation directory must be empty**.
3. **Package Permission**: Common users have the **execution permission** for the downloaded openGauss package.
4. **Port Check**: Before installation, check whether the specified openGauss port is occupied. If occupied, change the port number or stop the process using the port.

#### Simplified Single-Node Installation Procedure (`simpleInstall/install.sh`):
```bash
# 1. Decompress as common user (omm)
tar -jxf openGauss-2.0.0-openEuler-64bit.tar.bz2 -C /opt/software/openGauss
# 2. Go to simpleInstall directory and run install.sh
cd /opt/software/openGauss/simpleInstall
sh install.sh -w Huawei@123 -p 5432
```
- **`-w`**: Initializes the database password (passed to `gs_initdb`). **Mandatory** for security!
- **`-p`**: Specifies the openGauss port (**default is `5432`** if not specified).
- After installation, the default instance name is **`sgnode`**, and the data directory is `/opt/software/openGauss/data/single_node`.
- **Verification**:
  - `ps ux | grep gaussdb`
  - `gs_ctl query -D /opt/software/openGauss/data/single_node` (shows `local_role: Normal`, `db_state: Normal`).

---

### 2. Standard Enterprise XML Installation & Start/Stop Lifecycle (pp. 82, 94)
1. **Standard Flow**: Prepare OS -> Obtain package -> Configure **XML file** -> Decompress -> Run **`gs_preinstall`** (as `root` to initialize environment, check permissions, and create `omm`/`dbgrp`) -> Switch to `omm` and run **`gs_install -X clusterconfig.xml`** -> (Optional) Set standby node to readable.
2. **Starting and Stopping openGauss (as `omm`)**:
   - **Start cluster**: `gs_om -t start` (default timeout is **300s**; customize via `gs_om -t start --time-out=300`).
   - **Stop cluster**: `gs_om -t stop`
   - *Note*: An HA cluster must be started in HA mode. If started in standalone mode, restore the HA relationship using `gs_ctl build`.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss End-to-End Installation Pipeline (Official Reference: p. 82)](./assets/images/p3_h2s1_install_flowchart.png)
*Figure: openGauss End-to-End Installation Pipeline (Official Reference: p. 82)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. Uninstalling openGauss & Cleaning Up the Environment (pp. 124–125)
Uninstallation is a two-phase process:
1. **Phase 1 — Uninstall openGauss Application (as OS user `omm`)**:
   - Cluster-wide uninstallation: `gs_uninstall --delete-data`
   - Local single-node uninstallation: `gs_uninstall --delete-data -L`
   - Logs are saved to `$GAUSSLOG/om/gs_uninstall-YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS.log`.
2. **Phase 2 — One-Click Environment Cleanup (as user `root` ONLY)**:
   - Run **`gs_postuninstall -U omm -X clusterconfig.xml --delete-user --delete-group`** to clean up the OS environment settings made by `gs_preinstall`.
key_takeaways: All 4 items in Ch.02 Quiz Q3 (user/group & OS/network, rwx on decompression & empty install dir, execute permission on package, and checking if the port is occupied) are mandatory prerequisites for single-node installation.
In simplified single-node installation (`sh install.sh -w <password>`), `-w` is mandatory, `-p` defaults to 5432, the database name is `sgnode`, and the data directory is `data/single_node`.
Uninstallation requires `gs_uninstall --delete-data` run as `omm`, followed by `gs_postuninstall` run as `root`.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.02 Quiz Q3): All four options (A, B, C, D) are correct prerequisites for installing openGauss on a single node!
EXAM TRAP: Only `root` is authorized to run `gs_preinstall`, `gs_checkos`, and `gs_postuninstall`, whereas `omm` runs `gs_install`, `gs_om`, and `gs_uninstall`.

lecture.title: Client Authentication (`pg_hba.conf`), `postgresql.conf` & `gsql` Connections
objectives: Configure client authentication policies in `pg_hba.conf` using `gs_guc set` and `gs_guc reload`
Distinguish `HOSTTYPE` (`local`, `host`, `hostssl`, `hostnossl`) and `AUTHMETHOD` (`sha256`, `md5`, `trust`, `reject`, `cert`, `gss`)
Inspect node IP and port (`gs_om -t status --detail`, `postgresql.conf`) and connect via `gsql`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Setting Client Authentication Policies in `pg_hba.conf` (p. 96, 118)
By default, parameters in `pg_hba.conf` and `postgresql.conf` are configured for standalone local access. Use **`gs_guc`** (as user `omm`) to modify parameters or host-based authentication policies:
```bash
gs_guc [ set | reload ] [-N NODE-NAME] [-I INSTANCE-NAME | -D DATADIR] \
  -h "HOSTTYPE DATABASE USERNAME IPADDR-WITH-IPMASK AUTHMETHOD [authentication-options]"
```
- **`set` vs. `reload`**:
  - **`set`**: Modifies **only** the parameter in the configuration file (requires restart or reload later).
  - **`reload`**: Modifies the parameter in the configuration file **AND sends semaphores (signals) to the database process** to reload the configuration file immediately without restarting!
  - *Removing a policy*: Omit `AUTHMETHOD`/`authentication-options` in `gs_guc ... -h "..."` to comment out an existing line in `pg_hba.conf`.

| Parameter | Supported Values & Technical Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| **`HOSTTYPE`** | **`local`** (Unix domain socket), **`host`** (plain or SSL TCP/IP socket), **`hostssl`** (SSL-encrypted TCP/IP socket only), **`hostnossl`** (non-SSL TCP/IP socket only). |
| **`AUTHMETHOD`** | **`sha256`** (SHA-256 password hash, **recommended**), **`md5`** (MD5 hash, not supported by default), **`trust`** (no password check; **remote hosts are NOT allowed to use `trust`**), **`reject`** (unconditionally reject connection), **`cert`** (SSL client certificate), **`gss`** (Kerberos authentication). |

---

### 2. Confirming Connection Info & Connecting with `gsql` (pp. 97–99)
1. **Query Primary Node IP & Data Directory**:
   ```bash
   gs_om -t status --detail
   ```
2. **Check Port in `postgresql.conf`**:
   ```bash
   cat /srv/BigData/gaussdb/data1/dbnode/postgresql.conf | grep port
   # port = 8000 (or 5432 in simpleInstall)
   ```
3. **Connect Locally or Remotely with `gsql`**:
   ```bash
   gsql -d postgres -p 8000
   # Remote connection: gsql -h 192.168.0.11 -d postgres -p 8000 -U jack -W Bigdata@123
   ```
   - **Prompt Indicator**: Logging in as administrator `omm` displays **`postgres=#`** (`#` = superuser/admin); logging in as a common user displays **`postgres=>`** (`>` = normal user).
   - **Timeouts**:
     - **`session_timeout`**: Automatically disconnects an idle client session (set `session_timeout = 0` to disable idle timeouts).
     - **`gsql` connection timeout**: Fixed at **5 minutes** when establishing a connection and authenticating.
   - **Change Password & Exit**:
     ```sql
     ALTER ROLE omm IDENTIFIED BY 'NewPass@2026' REPLACE 'OldPass@2012';
     \q
     ```
key_takeaways: `gs_guc set` only writes to the config file, whereas `gs_guc reload` writes to the config file AND signals the database process to reload immediately.
In `pg_hba.conf`, `sha256` is the recommended authentication method; `trust` is only allowed for local connections (remote hosts cannot use `trust`).
In `gsql`, `DBNAME=#` indicates an administrator (`omm`) prompt, whereas `DBNAME=>` indicates a common user prompt.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Remote hosts are NOT allowed to access openGauss using `trust` mode in `pg_hba.conf`! Remote connections must use `sha256` (recommended), `cert`, or `gss`.

EXAM TRAP: System catalogs store structured metadata of openGauss. Never manually add, delete, or modify system catalogs, as doing so causes metadata inconsistency or database unavailability (Ch.02 p. 100).

lecture.title: openGauss Client & Server O&M Tools (`gsql`, `gs_check*`, `gs_dump*`, `gs_om`, `gs_ssh`)
objectives: Distinguish openGauss Client Tools (`gsql`) from Server Tools (`gs_check`, `gs_checkos`, `gs_checkperf`, `gs_clean`, `gs_collector`, `gs_dump`, `gs_dumpall`, `gs_guc`, `gs_om`, `gs_restore`, `gs_ssh`)
Identify which tool and check item require `root` privileges (`gs_checkos`, `gs_checkperf -i SSD`)
Master the key options of `gs_check`, `gs_checkos`, `gs_checkperf`, `gs_clean`, `gs_collector`, `gs_dump`, `gs_dumpall`, `gs_restore`, `gs_om`, and `gs_ssh`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Client Tools vs. Server Tools Classification (pp. 102–104, Ch.02 Quiz Q1!)
All tools are located in `GPHOME/script` and `GAUSSHOME/bin`.
- **Client Tool (ONLY ONE in this table!)**:
  - **`gsql`**: CLI database connection tool used by clients to connect to the server, run interactive/scripted SQL statements, and execute meta-commands (`\l`, `\c`, `\dt`, `\d`, `\q`). **(`gsql` is NOT a server tool — exact Ch.02 Quiz Q1: C!)**
- **11 Server Tools (p. 104)**:
  1. **`gs_check`**: Comprehensive environment check (OS, network, DB runtime) before major operations. Must specify **`-i ITEM`** (single item, e.g., `-i CheckCPU`) or **`-e SCENE_NAME`** (scenario: `inspect`, `upgrade`, `binary_upgrade`, `health`, `install`). Use `--skip-root-items` to skip root checks.
  2. **`gs_checkos`**: Checks OS version, kernel parameters, disk/I/O/network settings, and THP. **Only `root` is authorized to run `gs_checkos`!**
     - `-i A1..A14`: **Checks** OS parameters without modifying them.
     - `-i B1..B8`: **Sets** OS parameters to expected values (A and B items cannot be used simultaneously; `-f` and `-h` cannot be used together).
  3. **`gs_checkperf`**: Routinely checks performance at 4 levels:
     - **openGauss level** (Host/GaussDB CPU usage, shared memory hit rate, in-memory sort ratio, I/O, disk, transaction stats) — run as `omm` (`-i PMK`). *Note*: If PMK statistics are missing, run `ANALYZE pmk.pmk_snapshot;` etc.
     - **Host level** (CPU, memory, I/O usage) — run as `omm`.
     - **Session/Process level** (CPU, memory, shared buffer hits) — run as `omm`.
     - **SSD performance** (read every 7s / write every 10s via `dd flag=direct bs=8M count=2560`) — **Can be viewed ONLY by user `root` (`gs_checkperf -U omm -i SSD`)! (Exact Ch.02 Quiz Q2: D!)**
  4. **`gs_clean`**: Connects to the primary DN and clears residual temporary tables (`-a`/`--all`, `-e`/`--exclusive`) or rolls back abnormal two-phase transactions (`-r`/`--rollback`) after an unexpected crash. Default concurrency `-j` is 3 (range 1–10).
  5. **`gs_collector`**: Collects OS info, logs, and config files (`--begin-time`, `--end-time`, `--keyword`, `-C CONFIGFILE`) into a `.tar.gz` package when openGauss is faulty (depends on `gstack`).
  6. **`gs_dump`**: Exports a **single database** or its objects (schemas, tables, views) consistently without blocking user R/W (acquires shared lock; tune wait via `--lock-wait-timeout`). Supports 4 formats via **`-F`**:
     - **`p` (Plain-text SQL)**: Restore with **`gsql`** (recommended for small DBs).
     - **`c` (Custom binary)**: Medium compression by default; restore with **`gs_restore`** (recommended for medium/large DBs).
     - **`d` (Directory)** & **`t` (`.tar` archive, max 8 GB per table)**: Restore with **`gs_restore`**.
  7. **`gs_dumpall`**: Exports **all databases** in the cluster + **global objects** (roles/users, tablespaces, global permissions) as a **plain-text SQL script** (restore with **`gsql`**).
  8. **`gs_guc`**: Modifies `postgresql.conf` / `pg_hba.conf` (`check`, `set`, `reload`, `encrypt -M server|client|source` generating `.key.cipher` and `.key.rand`).
  9. **`gs_om`**: Cluster lifecycle & config maintenance (`-t start | stop | restart | status | generateconf | refreshconf | view | query | cert | kerberos`).
  10. **`gs_restore`**: Imports custom (`c`), directory (`d`), or `.tar` (`t`) archives exported by `gs_dump`. Imports incrementally by default; use **`-c`** to clean/drop existing objects before recreating.
  11. **`gs_ssh`**: Runs the same Linux shell command synchronously across all cluster nodes (`gs_ssh -c "cmd"`).
key_takeaways: `gsql` is a Client tool, NOT a Server tool (Ch.02 Quiz Q1).
When using `gs_checkperf`, SSD performance (`-i SSD`) can be viewed ONLY by user `root` (Ch.02 Quiz Q2). Similarly, `gs_checkos` can only be run by `root`.

`gs_dump` supports 4 formats (`p` plain-text restored via `gsql`; `c` custom, `d` directory, and `t` tar restored via `gs_restore`), whereas `gs_dumpall` exports only plain-text SQL scripts of all databases and global objects.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.02 Quiz Q1): 'Which of the following is not an openGauss server tool?' -> C. `gsql` (`gsql` is a client tool!).
EXAM TRAP (Ch.02 Quiz Q2): 'When the `gs_checkperf` tool is used to check system performance, which of the following can be viewed only by user `root`?' -> D. SSD performance!

lecture.title: Instance Architecture — Memory, Multi-Threading & Directory Layout
objectives: Distinguish Shared Memory (`shared_buffers`, `cstore_buffers`, `wal_buffers`, `MOT`) from Session/Local Memory (`work_mem`, `maintenance_work_mem`, `temp_buffers`)
Describe the roles of core openGauss threads (`GaussMaster`, `pagewriter`, `bgwriter`, `walwriter`, `checkpointer`, `WalSender`, `WalReceiver`)
Navigate the logical storage hierarchy (Tablespace -> Database -> Datafile Segment -> 8 KB Block) and physical data directory (`base`, `global`, `pg_xlog`, `pg_clog`, `pg_audit`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Memory Structure: Shared vs. Local Memory (pp. 135–137)

| Memory Region | Scope | Purpose & Tuning Guidance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`shared_buffers` (Shared buffer)** | Shared | Main memory cache bridging disk and CPU for row-store read/write operations. |
| **`cstore_buffers` (cstore buffer)** | Shared | Shared buffer dedicated to **column-store tables**. When using mostly column-store tables, reduce `shared_buffers` and increase `cstore_buffers`. |
| **`MOT` (Memory-Optimized Table)** | Shared / Local | Stores all MOT data and indexes in memory (`CREATE FOREIGN TABLE test(x int);`). Supports ACID with RC or RR isolation. |
| **`wal_buffers` (wal buffer)** | Shared | Shared memory staging area for Write-Ahead Logs (WALs) before flushing to disk. |
| **`maintenance_work_mem`** | Local (Session) | Local memory used for maintenance tasks: `VACUUM`, `CREATE INDEX`, and `ALTER TABLE`. |
| **`work_mem`** | Local (Session) | Local memory per query operator for **sorting (`Sort`)** and **hash tables (`HashJoin`/`HashAgg`)**. |
| **`temp_buffers` (temp buffer)** | Local (Session) | Session-private buffer for accessing **temporary tables**. |
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Instance Architecture (GaussMaster, Background Threads, Memory Pools, Storage) (Official Reference: p. 135)](./assets/images/p3_h3s1_instance_architecture.png)
*Figure: openGauss Instance Architecture (GaussMaster, Background Threads, Memory Pools, Storage) (Official Reference: p. 135)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Main Threads in `gaussdb` (pp. 135, 138)
- **`GaussMaster` (`postmaster`)**: Main management thread handling startup, shutdown, client connections, and message forwarding.
- **`pagewriter`**: Copies dirty pages to the **double-write (double-writer) space** and flushes them to disk (preventing torn-page corruption), then forwards dirty pages to `bgwriter` subthreads.
- **`bgwriter`**: Flushes dirty pages from `shared_buffers` to disk in the background so user query threads do not wait for free buffers and checkpoint spikes are smoothed.
- **`walwriter`**: Flushes WAL records from `wal_buffers` in memory to WAL files on disk to guarantee durability of committed transactions.
- **`checkpointer` (`checkpoint`)**: Periodically triggered to flush all dirty pages to disk and advance the recovery redo point.
- **Other Key Background Threads**: `WalSender` / `WalReceiver` (primary/standby WAL streaming), `AutoVacLauncher` (vacuuming), `Stat_collector` (statistics), `Auditor` (audit logs), `sysLogger` (run logs), `LWLockMonitor`.

---

### 3. Logical Architecture & Physical Directory Structure (pp. 141–144)
- **Logical Hierarchy**:
  - **Tablespace**: Physical directory mapping; one tablespace can store objects from multiple databases, and one database can span multiple tablespaces.
  - **Table & Datafile Segment**: Each table belongs to **only one database and one tablespace**. Each datafile segment belongs to only one table; **tables > 1 GB are split across multiple 1 GB datafile segments**.
  - **Block (Page)**: Basic unit of database I/O management; **default size is 8 KB**.
- **Physical Data Directory (`$GAUSSHOME/bin`, `lib`, `share`, and Instance Data Dir `0700`)**:
  - **`base/`**: Subdirectories for each database's tables/indexes.
  - **`global/`**: Cluster-wide system catalogs (e.g., `pg_database`, `pg_authid`, `pg_tablespace`).
  - **`pg_xlog/`**: Stores Write-Ahead Logs (WAL / redo logs).
  - **`pg_clog/` & `pg_csnlog/`**: Transaction commit status logs and Commit Sequence Number logs.
  - **`pg_audit/` & `pg_log/`**: Audit logs (`0600`) and instance run logs (`<= 0640`).
  - **`postgresql.conf` / `pg_hba.conf` / `postmaster.opts`**: Parameter file, client auth file, and startup CLI args.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Primary/Standby Logical Architecture (Official Reference: p. 139)](./assets/images/p3_h3s1_logical_primary_standby.png)
*Figure: openGauss Primary/Standby Logical Architecture (Official Reference: p. 139)*

![Database Logical Objects to Physical Datafile Segments and 8KB Blocks (Official Reference: p. 141)](./assets/images/p3_h3s1_db_physical_mapping.png)
*Figure: Database Logical Objects to Physical Datafile Segments and 8KB Blocks (Official Reference: p. 141)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: In openGauss logical storage, a table exceeding 1 GB is split into multiple 1 GB datafile segments, and the default block size is 8 KB.
`pagewriter` writes dirty pages to the double-writer space first to prevent torn-page corruption, while `walwriter` flushes WAL buffers to `pg_xlog`.

`base/` holds per-database subdirectories, `global/` holds cluster-wide tables, `pg_xlog/` holds WAL files, and directory permissions are `0750` (program), `0700` (data dir), and `0600` (data/audit files).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Column-store tables rarely use `shared_buffers`; they use `cstore_buffers`! For column-store workloads, decrease `shared_buffers` and increase `cstore_buffers` (Ch.03 p. 136).
EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse `pg_log` (instance runtime logs) with `pg_xlog` (Write-Ahead Logs / redo logs used for crash recovery) or `pg_clog` (transaction commit status logs).

lecture.title: Resource Pooling Architecture (DMS, DSS & Shared Storage)
objectives: Explain how openGauss Resource Pooling decouples Compute, Memory (DMS), and Storage (DSS)
List the hardware/protocol requirements (OceanStor Dorado SAN, SCSI3 PR & CAW, CX5 NIC, OCK RDMA) and feature limitations

Describe the 6 advanced Resource Pooling enhancements (Standby visibility/Xmin/snapshot caching, Transparent write forwarding, DSS thread pool/blackbox/NoF+, Operator offloading/NDP, Dual-cluster DR, On-demand replay, and SPQ multi-node parallel query)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Core Components of openGauss Resource Pooling (pp. 146–149)
Resource pooling innovates HA deployment by allowing **1 Read/Write Primary node and up to 7 Read-Only Standby nodes** to **share a single copy of underlying storage** while pooling memory across nodes for **real-time consistent reads** on standby nodes (`RPO = 0`, no delayed read under Read Committed):
1. **DSS (Distributed Storage Service)**:
   - Consists of **DSS Server** (an independent process that directly manages raw LUN devices of disk arrays like **OceanStor Dorado** and provides distributed file system semantics) and **DSS API** (a dynamic library integrated into `gaussdb` communicating with DSS Server via shared memory).
   - System catalog storage is switched from page mode to **segment-page mode** (supports **only segment-page tables**).
2. **DMS (Distributed Memory Service)**:
   - A dynamic library integrated into the database that pools memory and exchanges hot data pages in real time between primary and standby shared buffer pools over **TCP** (default) or **OCK RDMA** (with **CX5 NIC**, reducing standby consistent-read latency by **>= 20%**).
   - Log replication is **not** required between primary and standby nodes during normal operation because pages are exchanged directly via DMS!
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Resource Pooling Architecture (DMS, DSS and Shared Storage) (Official Reference: p. 146)](./assets/images/p3_h3s2_resource_pooling.png)
*Figure: openGauss Resource Pooling Architecture (DMS, DSS and Shared Storage) (Official Reference: p. 146)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Hardware Requirements & Feature Limitations (pp. 150–151)
- **Hardware Prerequisites**:
  - Disk array (e.g., **OceanStor Dorado 5000**) with **UltraPath** multipath software installed (**Ceph is NOT supported**).
  - LUNs must support **SCSI3 PR (`PR OUT`, `PR IN`, `INQUIRY`)** for cluster **I/O FENCE**, and **SCSI3 `CAW` (Compare and Write)** for shared disk locks.
  - Supports at most **1 primary node + 7 standby nodes** on the same disk array.
- **Feature Limitations in Resource Pooling Mode (p. 151)**:
  - **NOT supported**: Global temporary tables, Hash indexes, Cascaded standby nodes, Logical replication publication/subscription (`T_CreatePublicationStmt`, etc.), `gs_xlogdump_*` / `gs_repair_page` functions, and converting between traditional and resource-pooling deployments.

---

### 3. Seven Resource Pooling Performance & HA Enhancements (pp. 152–159)
1. **Standby Visibility & Snapshot Optimization (v5.1.0+, +50%–80% sysbench read perf)**:
   - Standby caches `XID -> CSN` mappings in its local L2 cache; Primary locally caches cluster `oldest Xmin` (standbys send local `oldest Xmin` periodically via background thread); Primary can broadcast latest snapshots to standbys.
2. **Transparent Write Forwarding on Standby (`write-on-standby`)**: Inside an explicit transaction (`BEGIN ... END`) on a standby node, read statements execute locally on the standby while write statements are transparently forwarded to the primary node.
3. **DSS Enhancements**: Thread pools for DSS Server, crash **black box logs** (`_LOG_LEVEL=0` to disable), and **NoF/NoF+** storage networking APIs.
4. **Operator Offloading / Near-Data Processing (NDP)**: Offloads `SeqScan`, `Filter`, `Projection`, and `Agg` operators to storage nodes to filter data before network transmission.
5. **Dual-Cluster DR**: Synchronizes Xlogs between a Primary Cluster and Standby Cluster via **Network Streaming Replication** (v6.0.0-RC1) or **OceanStor Dorado Synchronous Replication** (v5.1.0, intra-city 100 km, `RPO = 0`, `RTO < 30s`).
6. **On-Demand Replay for Ultimate RTO**: Because standbys in resource pooling do not continuously replay primary WAL logs, upon primary failure the promoted standby rebuilds only essential metadata so services resume immediately, replaying remaining logs on-demand in the background.
7. **Multi-Node Parallelism (SPQ — Shared-Everything Parallel Query, v6.0.0-RC1)**: Integrates the **ORCA optimizer** to distribute a single large OLAP query across all read nodes in parallel using virtual Node-Groups.
key_takeaways: Resource Pooling relies on DSS (Distributed Storage Service — DSS Server process + DSS API dynamic library) for shared disk array storage and DMS (Distributed Memory Service) for real-time TCP/RDMA page exchange.

Resource Pooling supports up to 1 Primary + 7 Standby nodes, requires SCSI3 PR (for I/O Fence) and SCSI3 CAW (for shared disk locks) on disk arrays like OceanStor Dorado, and supports ONLY segment-page tables.
Global temporary tables, hash indexes, and cascaded standby nodes are NOT supported in resource pooling mode.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse DMS (Distributed Memory Service, a dynamic library inside the database for cross-node page exchange) with DSS (Distributed Storage Service, which includes an independent DSS Server process managing raw LUNs).
EXAM TRAP: In Resource Pooling mode, standby nodes do NOT replay logs during normal operation — they exchange pages via DMS and use On-Demand Replay during failover to achieve Ultimate RTO.

lecture.title: Optimizers (CBO vs ABO), Statistics (`ANALYZE`) & Row-Store vs Column-Store
objectives: Compare the Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO, v1.0.0+) and AI-Based Optimizer (ABO, v3.1.0+)
Collect single-column and multi-column statistics using `ANALYZE` and inspect `PG_STATISTIC` / `PG_CLASS`
Contrast Row-Store and Column-Store tables (`WITH (ORIENTATION = COLUMN, COMPRESSION = ...)` — Ch.04 Quiz Q3)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Query Optimizers: CBO vs. ABO (pp. 161–166)
- **CBO (Cost-Based Optimizer, introduced in v1.0.0)**:
  - Consists of **3 key components**:
    1. **Query converter**: Rewrites SQL statements into lower-cost equivalent forms.
    2. **Cost estimator**: Calculates execution cost based on table tuples, column width, NULL ratio, distinct count, and **MCV (`most_common_vals`)**.
    3. **Execution plan generator**: Explores access paths, join methods, and join orders to pick the lowest-cost plan.
- **ABO (AI-Based Optimizer, 3rd-gen intelligent optimizer introduced in v3.1.0)**:
  - **Sub-feature 1 — Intelligent Cardinality Estimation**: Uses a **Bayesian network (`BAYESNET`)** model to capture joint distributions across correlated/skewed columns for multi-column equality queries.
    - Enable via GUC: `SET enable_ai_stats = on; SET multi_stats_type = 'BAYESNET';` (or `'ALL'`), then run `ANALYZE`.
  - **Sub-feature 2 — Adaptive Plan Selection**: Maintains multiple cached execution plans using range linear expansion and range coverage matching (especially for partial indexes and offsets) rather than a single rigid generic cached plan.

---

### 2. Statistics Collection (`ANALYZE`) & `PG_STATISTIC` (pp. 167–170)
- **Where Statistics Live**:
  - **`pg_class`**: Stores global table-level **`relpages`** (disk pages) and **`reltuples`** (estimated rows).
  - **`pg_statistic`**: Stores column-level statistics (`starelid`, `staattnum`, `stanullfrac` [NULL ratio], `stawidth` [avg byte width], `stadistinct` [distinct values], `stanumbersN`, `stavaluesN`, `histogram_bounds`). Accessible **only to system administrators** (ordinary users query the `PG_STATS` view if authorized).
- **Sampling Rule**: By default, `default_statistics_target = 100` samples **30,000 rows**. If a table exceeds **1,600,000 rows**, Huawei recommends setting `default_statistics_target = -2` (which samples **2%** of the rows).
- **Commands**:
  ```sql
  ANALYZE tablename;                                    -- Single table
  ANALYZE;                                              -- Entire database
  ANALYZE tablename (col_1, col_2);                     -- Specific columns
  ALTER TABLE tablename ADD STATISTICS ((col_1, col_2)); -- Declare multi-column stats for future ANALYZE
  ```

---

### 3. Row-Store vs. Column-Store Tables (pp. 171–173, 296–301, Ch.04 Quiz Q3!)

| Feature | Row-Store Table (`ORIENTATION = ROW`, Default) | Column-Store Table (`ORIENTATION = COLUMN`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Storage Layout** | All attributes of a row are stored contiguously together | Values of the same column across rows are stored together |
| **Strengths** | Fast **`INSERT` / `UPDATE` / `DELETE`**; fast **point queries** (index lookup returning a few rows) or `SELECT *` | High **compression ratio**; efficient **projection** (reads only queried columns, drastically reducing disk I/O) |
| **Weaknesses** | Reading 2 columns out of 50 still reads the entire row from disk | Tuple reconstruction overhead; **inefficient for frequent single-row `INSERT`/`UPDATE` and point queries** |
| **Best Scenario** | **OLTP**: frequent small writes/updates and point queries | **OLAP**: batch inserts, statistical aggregations (`SUM`/`GROUP BY`), wide tables where queries touch **< 50% of columns** |

```sql
CREATE TABLE sales_col (id INT, region VARCHAR(20), amount NUMERIC(10,2))
WITH (ORIENTATION = COLUMN, COMPRESSION = HIGH);
```
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Row-Store vs Column-Store Storage Model Visual Comparison (Official Reference: p. 171)](./assets/images/p3_h3s3_row_vs_column_store.png)
*Figure: Row-Store vs Column-Store Storage Model Visual Comparison (Official Reference: p. 171)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: A CBO consists of three components: Query converter, Cost estimator, and Execution plan generator.
ABO (v3.1.0+) introduces Bayesian Network (`BAYESNET`) intelligent multi-column cardinality estimation (`enable_ai_stats = on`) and Adaptive Plan Selection.

Row-store (default) excels at frequent INSERT/UPDATE and point queries; Column-store (`WITH (ORIENTATION = COLUMN)`) excels at compression, projection, and OLAP statistical aggregations (Ch.04 Quiz Q3: ABC).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.04 Quiz Q3): Statement D claims 'Row-store tables are used in scenarios where there are a large number of queries for statistical analysis.' FALSE! Statistical analysis queries over massive data use Column-store tables (Answer: ABC).
EXAM TRAP: The `PG_STATISTIC` system catalog is accessible ONLY to system administrators; non-admin users must use authorized views (`PG_STATS`).

lecture.title: Table Partitioning, Kunpeng NUMA Optimization, SMP & High Availability / Ultimate RTO
objectives: Create and manage Range, List, and Hash partitioned tables and `LOCAL`/`GLOBAL` partitioned indexes
Explain Kunpeng 920 NUMA optimizations (`numactl -H`, ARMv8.1 `casal` atomic instruction, core binding) and SMP (`query_dop`)
Execute Primary/Standby `switchover` vs `failover` (`gs_ctl`, `gs_om -t refreshconf`), configure Ultimate RTO (`recovery_parse_workers`, `recovery_parallelism`), and describe Logical Replication
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Table Partitioning (pp. 174–181)
openGauss horizontally splits a table into non-overlapping physical partitions to deliver **high query efficiency (partition pruning)**, **high availability**, **easy maintenance**, and **balanced I/O**:
- **3 Partitioning Modes**:
  1. **Range Partitioning (`PARTITION BY RANGE(col)`)**: Maps rows by non-overlapping value ranges (`VALUES LESS THAN (...)`). Most common (often on time/date columns).
  2. **List Partitioning (`PARTITION BY LIST(col)`)**: Maps rows by discrete key value lists (`VALUES (...)`).
  3. **Hash Partitioning (`PARTITION BY HASH(col)`)**: Maps rows evenly across partitions using an internal hash function.
- **Core Partition DDL Operations (pp. 177–180)**:
  ```sql
  ALTER TABLE student1 ADD PARTITION score4 VALUES LESS THAN (101);
  ALTER TABLE student1 DROP PARTITION score1;
  ALTER TABLE student1 RENAME PARTITION score2 TO score2_new;
  ALTER TABLE student1 TRUNCATE PARTITION score2_new;
  SELECT * FROM student1 PARTITION (score2_new);
  CREATE INDEX student1_index1 ON student1 (score) LOCAL;
  ALTER INDEX student1_index2 RENAME PARTITION score1_index TO score1_index_new;
  ```

---

### 2. Kunpeng NUMA Architecture Optimization & SMP Parallelism (pp. 182–188)
- **Kunpeng 920 NUMA Structure (p. 183)**:
  - A 2-socket Kunpeng 920 (64 cores, 2 Dies per socket = **4 NUMA nodes 0–3**) has local node access distance **10**, intra-socket cross-die distance **16** (1.6x latency), and cross-socket distance **25–33**. Inspect via **`numactl -H`**.
  - **5 openGauss NUMA Optimizations (pp. 182–186)**:
    1. **Thread-to-Core Binding**: Separately binds network interrupts and service threads to CPU cores to prevent cross-core thread migration.
    2. **NUMA-Aware Data Structures**: Partitions hotspot structures (e.g., Clog partitions, WAL buffers) per NUMA node to reduce cross-node access.
    3. **Redo Log Batch Insertion** & larger Kunpeng L3 cache-line padding.
    4. **ARMv8.1 LSE Atomic Instruction (`casal`)**: Replaces 4 instructions (`ldxr` + `stlxr` loop) with **1 single atomic instruction (`casal`)**, boosting 2-socket Kunpeng TPC-C performance by **> 10%** (from **1.34M to 1.51M tpmC**)!
- **SMP (Symmetric Multi-Processing, pp. 187–188)**:
  - Intra-query operator-level multi-threaded parallel execution within a single process (exchanging data in memory via the **`Stream`** operator without network overhead).
  - Controlled by GUC **`query_dop`**: `1` (disabled, default); `0` (adaptive selection between `[1, 8]` when system load < 50%). *Note*: Data skew or high concurrent OLTP load degrades SMP efficiency.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Kunpeng NUMA CPU Die Structure and Node Distance Matrix (Official Reference: p. 183)](./assets/images/p3_h3s4_kunpeng_numa_matrix.png)
*Figure: Kunpeng NUMA CPU Die Structure and Node Distance Matrix (Official Reference: p. 183)*

![NUMA-Aware Kernel Data Partitioning Structure (Official Reference: p. 185)](./assets/images/p3_h3s4_numa_kernel_struct.png)
*Figure: NUMA-Aware Kernel Data Partitioning Structure (Official Reference: p. 185)*

![Unscheduled Thread Migration vs NUMA-Pinned Core Binding (Official Reference: p. 186)](./assets/images/p3_h3s4_numa_thread_binding.png)
*Figure: Unscheduled Thread Migration vs NUMA-Pinned Core Binding (Official Reference: p. 186)*

![SMP Multi-Thread Parallel Execution Flow (Official Reference: p. 187)](./assets/images/p3_h3s4_smp_parallel.png)
*Figure: SMP Multi-Thread Parallel Execution Flow (Official Reference: p. 187)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. High Availability, Switchover/Failover, Ultimate RTO & Logical Replication (pp. 190–198)
- **Switchover vs. Failover (pp. 190–193)**:
  - **Switchover (Planned maintenance, zero data loss)**:
    ```bash
    gs_om -t status --detail
    gs_ctl switchover -D /home/omm/cluster/dn1/   # Run on target standby node as omm
    gs_om -t refreshconf                          # Save dynamic primary/standby role state
    ```
  - **Failover (Unplanned primary fault, may cause data loss if async)**:
    ```bash
    gs_ctl failover -D /home/omm/cluster/dn1/     # Promote standby to primary
    gs_om -t refreshconf
    ```
  - *Cascaded standby rule*: Cannot be directly promoted to primary; must first switchover/failover to become a normal standby, then primary.
- **RPO vs. RTO & Ultimate RTO (pp. 195–197)**:
  - **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**: Data-oriented — maximum tolerable period of **data loss** (measures data integrity).
  - **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**: Application-oriented — maximum tolerable **service downtime** (measures recovery timeliness).
  - **Ultimate RTO (Parallel Redo + Incremental Checkpoint)**: Uses multi-level pipelines to replay Xlogs in parallel on the standby node. Enabled only when **both `recovery_parse_workers > 1` AND `recovery_parallelism > 1`**. *(Constraint: Cascaded standby nodes are NOT supported when Ultimate RTO is enabled!)*
- **Logical Replication (p. 198)**: DNs reversely parse physical WAL logs into logical logs (**logical decoding**, supported on standby nodes since v1.1.0); tools like **DRS** convert them into SQL for heterogeneous bidirectional sync with **MySQL** or **Oracle**. *(Constraint: Column-store replication is NOT supported!)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![RPO vs RTO Disaster Recovery Metrics on Time Axis (Official Reference: p. 196)](./assets/images/p3_h3s4_rpo_vs_rto_timeline.png)
*Figure: RPO vs RTO Disaster Recovery Metrics on Time Axis (Official Reference: p. 196)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->
key_takeaways: On Kunpeng 920 (ARMv8.1 LSE), replacing `ldxr`/`stlxr` (4 instructions) with the single atomic `casal` instruction boosts TPC-C throughput from 1.34M to 1.51M tpmC (+10%).
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is data-oriented (tolerable data loss), whereas RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is application-oriented (tolerable service downtime).
After running `gs_ctl switchover -D <datadir>` or `gs_ctl failover -D <datadir>` on the standby node, you MUST run `gs_om -t refreshconf` to update the dynamic configuration file.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Parallel recovery (Ultimate RTO) is active ONLY when BOTH `recovery_parse_workers > 1` and `recovery_parallelism > 1`, and cascaded standby nodes are NOT supported when Ultimate RTO is enabled (Ch.03 p. 192 & p. 196).
EXAM TRAP: Logical replication supports row-store tables and standby decoding, but Column-store replication is NOT supported (Ch.03 p. 198).

lecture.title: High Security Part 1 — Fully-Encrypted Database & Dynamic Data Masking
objectives: Explain the 3-layer key hierarchy (Root Key, CMK, CEK) and workflow of Fully-Encrypted Equality Queries
Create Resource Labels (`CREATE RESOURCE LABEL`) and Dynamic Data Masking Policies (`CREATE MASKING POLICY`)
Compare all 7 preset masking functions (`creditcardmasking`, `basicemailmasking`, `fullemailmasking`, `alldigitsmasking`, `shufflemasking`, `randommasking`, `maskall`) and their constraints
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Equality Query in a Fully-Encrypted Database (pp. 56, 200–204)
Protects data privacy across its **entire lifecycle (transmission, computing, and storage)** so data on the server is always in ciphertext — even cloud admins or attackers with root access cannot read plaintext data:
- **3-Layer Key Hierarchy & Workflow (p. 201)**:
  1. **Root Key (RK)**: Managed locally via `keytool` on the client host.
  2. **Client Master Key (`CMK`)**: Stored on the client side and registered in the database metadata; used to encrypt the CEK.
  3. **Column Encryption Key (`CEK`)**: Encrypted by the CMK on the client and stored as ciphertext on the server; used by the **client driver (`ODBC`/`JDBC`/`gsql -C`)** to encrypt/decrypt column data.
  - **Encryption Types (`enc_type`)**: **`DETERMINISTIC`** (supports equality queries `=`; server column type becomes `BYTEAWITHOUTORDERWITHEQUALCOL`) vs. **`RANDOMIZED`** (higher security, non-deterministic ciphertext).
  - **Hardware TEE Support**: Can leverage Intel SGX / Huawei Kunpeng ARM **TEE (`secGear`)** for isolated computation.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Fully-Encrypted Database Equality Query (Client Driver to TEE) (Official Reference: p. 56)](./assets/images/p3_h1s4_fully_encrypted_tee.png)
*Figure: openGauss Fully-Encrypted Database Equality Query (Client Driver to TEE) (Official Reference: p. 56)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Dynamic Data Masking (pp. 205–208)
Masks sensitive column data dynamically at query time (`SELECT`) based on the user's identity (`ROLES`), client tool (`APP`), and IP (`IP`) **without modifying the underlying stored data**:
```sql
-- Step 1: Create Resource Labels on target table columns
CREATE RESOURCE LABEL label_for_creditcard ADD COLUMN(user1.table1.creditcard);
CREATE RESOURCE LABEL label_for_name ADD COLUMN(user1.table1.name);

-- Step 2: Create Masking Policies bound to Resource Labels
CREATE MASKING POLICY msk_creditcard creditcardmasking ON LABEL(label_for_creditcard);
CREATE MASKING POLICY msk_name randommasking ON LABEL(label_for_name)
    FILTER ON IP(local), ROLES(dev);
```

---

### 3. Seven Preconfigured Masking Functions & Constraints (pp. 207–208)

| Preset Masking Function | Masking Rule | Official Example (`Input` -> `Output`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`creditcardmasking`** | Masks all digits **except the last 4 digits** with `'x'` | `'4880-9898-4545-2525'` -> **`'xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-2525'`** |
| **`basicemailmasking`** | Masks all text **before `@`** with `'x'` | `'abcd@mymail.com'` -> **`'xxxx@mymail.com'`** |
| **`fullemailmasking`** | Masks text **before the first dot (`.`) (except `@`)** with `'x'` | `'abcd@gmail.com'` -> **`'xxxx@xxxxx.com'`** |
| **`alldigitsmasking`** | Masks **only digits** with `'0'` | `'alex123alex'` -> **`'alex000alex'`** |
| **`shufflemasking`** | Randomly shuffles character positions (weak masking) | `'hello world'` -> **`'hlwoeor dl'`** |
| **`randommasking`** | Randomly replaces each character | `'hello world'` -> **`'ad5f5ghdf5'`** |
| **`maskall`** | Replaces every character with `'x'` | `'4880-9898-4545-2525'` -> **`'xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx'`** |

- **Key Constraints (p. 208)**:
  - Must be created by **`POLADMIN`**, **`SYSADMIN`**, or the **initial user** (with GUC `enable_security_policy = on`).
  - Maximum of **98 dynamic data masking policies**; only the **7 preset masking functions** above can be used.
  - Applies **only to `COLUMN` resource labels on base tables** and takes effect **only on `SELECT`** queries (Note: `INSERT INTO ... SELECT` or `MERGE INTO` from a masked source column permanently writes the **masked value**!).
key_takeaways: In a Fully-Encrypted Database, the Client Master Key (CMK) encrypts the Column Encryption Key (CEK), and the client driver encrypts/decrypts data so the server only ever sees ciphertext.
Dynamic Data Masking uses Resource Labels (`CREATE RESOURCE LABEL ... ADD COLUMN(...)`) and Masking Policies (`CREATE MASKING POLICY ... ON LABEL(...)`) and supports 7 preset functions.
`basicemailmasking` masks only before `@` (`xxxx@gmail.com`), whereas `fullemailmasking` masks everything before the last domain dot except `@` (`xxxx@xxxxx.com`).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Dynamic Data Masking can only be created by a user with `POLADMIN`, `SYSADMIN`, or initial user privileges, supports at most 98 policies, and only masks `SELECT` queries on base table columns.
EXAM TRAP: If a user subject to dynamic masking runs `INSERT INTO t2 SELECT masked_col FROM t1`, the inserted data in `t2` is the MASKED value and cannot be restored!

lecture.title: High Security Part 2 — RBAC, Row-Level Security (RLS), Unified Auditing & TDE
objectives: Explain RBAC (Who, What, How) and Separation of Duties (System, Security, and Audit Administrators)
Configure Row-Level Security (`ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, `CREATE ROW LEVEL SECURITY POLICY`) and understand its constraints
Create Unified Audit Policies (`CREATE AUDIT POLICY`) and Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) tables (`AES_128_CTR` / `SM4_CTR`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Access Control: RBAC & Separation of Duties (pp. 209–212)
- **Separation of Duties (3 Admin Roles, p. 209)**:
  1. **Security Administrator (`CREATEROLE`)**: Creates and manages users.
  2. **System Administrator (`SYSADMIN`)**: Grants and revokes user permissions.
  3. **Audit Administrator (`AUDITADMIN`)**: Audits all user behaviors.
- **RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)**:
  - Defines relationships among **Who** (subject/user/role), **What** (target database object), and **How** (specific positive/negative permission).
  - Supports many-to-many mappings (users <-> roles <-> permissions) and enforces the **principle of least privilege**.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) User-Role-Permission Mapping (Official Reference: p. 210)](./assets/images/p3_h4s2_rbac_model.png)
*Figure: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) User-Role-Permission Mapping (Official Reference: p. 210)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Row-Level Security (RLS, pp. 213–215)
Controls data visibility **row by row** so different users executing the exact same SQL statement see only the rows permitted by policy expressions (`PERMISSIVE` combined via `OR`, or `RESTRICTIVE` combined via `AND`):
```sql
ALTER TABLE tablename ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE ROW LEVEL SECURITY POLICY tablename_rls ON tablename USING(role = CURRENT_USER);
```
- **RLS Constraints (p. 215)**:
  - Applies **ONLY to `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`** operations (**cannot** be applied to `INSERT` or `MERGE`!).
  - Cannot be defined on **views**, **foreign tables (MOT)**, or **temporary tables**.
  - Maximum of **100 RLS policies** per table.
  - **Initial users and `SYSADMIN` users bypass (are not affected by) RLS policies.**

---

### 3. Unified Auditing & Transparent Data Encryption (TDE, pp. 216–226)
- **Unified Auditing (pp. 217–224)**:
  - Requires `enable_security_policy = on` and user with **`POLADMIN`**, **`SYSADMIN`**, or **initial user** privileges; logs via OS **`rsyslog`**.
  - **Syntax**:
    ```sql
    CREATE RESOURCE LABEL adt_lb0 ADD TABLE(tb_for_audit);
    -- DDL audit policy (PRIVILEGES)
    CREATE AUDIT POLICY adt3 PRIVILEGES CREATE ON LABEL(adt_lb0) FILTER ON ROLES(dev_audit, bob_audit);
    -- DML audit policy (ACCESS)
    CREATE AUDIT POLICY adt4 ACCESS SELECT ON LABEL(adt_lb0), INSERT ON LABEL(adt_lb0), DELETE
        FILTER ON ROLES(dev_audit, bob_audit), APP(psql, gsql), IP('10.20.30.40', '127.0.0.0/24');
    ```
  - **4 System Catalogs (p. 223)**: `GS_AUDITING_POLICY` (main info), `GS_AUDITING_POLICY_ACCESS` (DML), `GS_AUDITING_POLICY_PRIVILEGES` (DDL), `GS_AUDITING_POLICY_FILTERS` (filters).
  - **Constraint (p. 224)**: A single unified audit policy **cannot contain both DDL (`PRIVILEGES`) and DML (`ACCESS`) operations**! Max **98** unified audit policies.
- **Transparent Data Encryption (TDE, pp. 225–226)**:
  - Encrypts data automatically when writing to storage media and decrypts when reading, preventing static data file leakage.
  - **3-Layer Key Hierarchy (interconnected with Huawei Cloud KMS)**: **Root Key (`RK`)** -> **Cluster Master Key (`CMK`)** -> **Data Encryption Key (`DEK`, one per table, stored in `pg_class.reloptions`)**.
  - Supports **Heap Row-Store tables only** (does **not** support column-store, Ustore, materialized views, indexes, sequences, Xlogs, or MOTs).
  - Algorithms: **`AES_128_CTR` (default)** or **`SM4_CTR`**. Once specified at `CREATE TABLE`, the algorithm **cannot** be changed (and an unencrypted table created without TDE cannot later be converted to an encrypted table), though **DEK key rotation** is supported.
key_takeaways: Row-Level Security (RLS) affects ONLY `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` (not `INSERT` or `MERGE`), supports up to 100 policies per table, and does not affect initial users or `SYSADMIN`.
A single Unified Audit Policy (`CREATE AUDIT POLICY`) can audit either DDL (`PRIVILEGES`) or DML (`ACCESS`), but CANNOT contain both DDL and DML operations in the same policy.
TDE uses a 3-layer key hierarchy (RK -> CMK -> DEK via KMS) with `AES_128_CTR` (default) or `SM4_CTR` on heap row-store tables only.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Can a single Unified Audit Policy contain both `PRIVILEGES CREATE` (DDL) and `ACCESS SELECT` (DML)? NO! A unified audit policy applies to either DDL or DML, never both (Ch.03 p. 224).
EXAM TRAP: If a table is created without TDE enabled, it CANNOT later be switched to an encrypted table (only tables created with encryption can toggle encryption state or rotate DEKs, Ch.03 p. 225).
