lecture.title: Easy Maintenance — WDR Reports, One-Click Log Collection, Slow SQL & Session Diagnosis
objectives: Enable and generate Workload Diagnosis Reports (WDR) using `enable_wdr_snapshot`, `create_wdr_snapshot()`, and `generate_wdr_report()`
Distinguish WDR Summary vs. Detail report sections and configure Slow SQL diagnosis (`log_min_duration_statement`, `track_stmt_stat_level`, `statement_history`)
Diagnose blocked sessions and top wait events using `pg_thread_wait_status` and `DBE_PERF.local_active_session`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Workload Diagnosis Report (WDR, pp. 228–233)
WDR compares performance data between **two snapshots (`>= 2` snapshots required)** to diagnose long-term kernel performance bottlenecks:
- **Key GUC Parameters (p. 230)**:
  - **`enable_wdr_snapshot`**: Default is **`off`** (must be set to **`on`**).
  - **`wdr_snapshot_interval`**: Automatic background snapshot interval; default is **1 hour**.
  - **`wdr_snapshot_retention_days`**: Snapshot retention period; default is **8 days**.
- **Generating a WDR HTML Report (pp. 230–231)**:
  ```sql
  SELECT * FROM snapshot.snapshot;          -- View existing snapshot IDs
  SELECT create_wdr_snapshot();             -- Manually create a snapshot (sysadmin only)
  \a \t \o /home/om/wdrTestNode.html        -- Unaligned, tuples-only, redirect output to file
  SELECT generate_wdr_report(1, 2, 'all', 'node', 'dn_6001_6002');
  \o \a \t                                  -- Close output file & restore formatting
  ```
  - `report_type`: `'summary'`, `'detail'`, or `'all'`; `report_scope`: `'cluster'` or `'node'`.
- **Summary vs. Detail Report Contents (pp. 232–233)**:
  - **Summary Report**: `Database Stat`, `Load Profile` (incl. SQL P85/P90 response time), `Instance Efficiency Percentages` (cache hit ratio), `Events`, `Wait Classes` (`STATUS`, `LWLOCK_EVENT`, `LOCK_EVENT`, `IO_EVENT`), `CPU`, `I/O Profile`, `Memory Statistics`.
  - **Detail Report**: `Time Model`, `SQL Statistics`, `Wait Events`, `Cache I/O Stats`, `Utility status`, `Object stats`, `Configuration settings`.

---

### 2. One-Click Collection & Slow SQL Diagnosis (pp. 234–238)
- **One-Click Diagnosis Collection**: Extracts OS info, system catalogs/views, run/cluster logs, config files, core dumps, stack/trace info, and redo logs (xlogs) for rapid fault demarcation.
- **Slow SQL Diagnosis (v3.1.0+, pp. 236–238)**:
  - Records SQL jobs whose execution time exceeds **`log_min_duration_statement`**, controlled by **`track_stmt_stat_level`** (default `'OFF,L0'` — part 1 is Full SQL, part 2 is Slow SQL).
  - **Primary vs. Standby Querying**:
    - On the **Primary node**, query the **`statement_history`** table (must be queried inside the **`postgres`** database; empty in other DBs) or `DBE_PERF.get_global_full_sql_by_timestamp(start_ts, end_ts)`.
    - On the **Standby node** (which cannot write to tables), query the function **`dbe_perf.standby_statement_history`** inside the **`postgres`** database (memory/disk bounded by `track_stmt_standby_chain_size`).
    - Decode the binary `details` column via `pg_catalog.statement_detail_decode(details, 'plaintext', true)`. Sensitive query parameters in plans are automatically masked (`Filter: (name = '***'::text)`).

---

### 3. Active Session Performance Diagnosis (pp. 239–242)
Samples active sessions at 2 levels: **Level 1 (in-memory real-time, last few minutes)** and **Level 2 (persistent disk history)**:
```sql
-- 1. Check session blocking relationships
SELECT sessionid, block_sessionid FROM pg_thread_wait_status;
-- 2. Check blocked session and final blocker in active session samples
SELECT sessionid, block_sessionid, final_block_sessionid FROM DBE_PERF.local_active_session;
```
key_takeaways: Generating a WDR report requires `enable_wdr_snapshot = on` (default `off`) and at least 2 snapshots (`create_wdr_snapshot()` can only be run by `sysadmin`). Default interval is 1 hour and retention is 8 days.

Slow SQL diagnosis records queries exceeding `log_min_duration_statement` (controlled by `track_stmt_stat_level`, default `'OFF,L0'`), and `statement_history` / `dbe_perf.standby_statement_history` must be queried in the `postgres` database.
Session blocking relationships are inspected via `pg_thread_wait_status` and `DBE_PERF.local_active_session`.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: If you query `statement_history` (or `dbe_perf.standby_statement_history` on a standby node) in any database other than `postgres`, the result is empty or unavailable (Ch.03 p. 238)!
EXAM TRAP: `enable_wdr_snapshot` is `off` by default, and at least 2 snapshots must exist before `generate_wdr_report()` can generate a report.

lecture.title: AI Capabilities — AI4DB (`X-Tuner`, `SQLdiag`, `Index-advisor`) & DB4AI (`DeepSQL`, Native DB4AI)
objectives: Distinguish the two sub-pillars of DBMind: AI4DB (X-Tuner, SQLdiag, Index-advisor, Anomaly-detection) and DB4AI (DeepSQL, Native DB4AI)
Operate X-Tuner (`recommend`, `train`, `tune`), SQLdiag (`train`, `predict`), and Index-advisor (`gs_index_advise`, `hypopg_create_index`, `index_advisor_workload.py`)
Describe DeepSQL (60+ ML/graph algorithms) and Native DB4AI (`CREATE MODEL`, `PREDICT BY`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. openGauss AI Architecture (`DBMind`: `AI4DB` + `DB4AI`, p. 244)
- **AI4DB (AI for Database)**: Uses AI to make the database self-tuning, self-diagnosing, self-healing, and self-securing. Includes **`X-Tuner`**, **`SQLdiag`**, **`Index-advisor`**, and **`Anomaly-detection`**.
- **DB4AI (Database for AI)**: Runs machine learning and deep learning directly inside the database engine using SQL-like syntax without moving data across platforms. Includes **`DeepSQL`** and the **`Native DB4AI Engine`**.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss AI4DB (Self-Tuning, Diagnosis) and DB4AI Full Stack (Official Reference: p. 244)](./assets/images/p3_h4s4_ai_overview.png)
*Figure: openGauss AI4DB (Self-Tuning, Diagnosis) and DB4AI Full Stack (Official Reference: p. 244)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. AI4DB Tools: `X-Tuner`, `SQLdiag` & `Index-advisor` (pp. 245–263)

#### A. `X-Tuner` (Knob Parameter Tuning Tool, pp. 245–249)
- Uses **Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL, e.g., DDPG)** and **Global Search Algorithms (Bayesian optimization, Particle Swarm Optimization / PSO)**. Can be run from source (`python main.py`) or installed via `python setup.py install` (`gs_xtuner`).
- **3 Running Modes (p. 247)**:
  1. **`recommend`**: Inspects current workload features and generates a parameter recommendation report **in seconds without restarting the database**.
  2. **`train`**: Iteratively modifies knobs and runs benchmarks to train a DRL model (may restart DB repeatedly).
  3. **`tune`**: Tunes parameters using either a trained DRL model (requires `train` first with identical knob list/min/max) or a Global Search algorithm (no pre-training required).

#### B. `SQLdiag` (SQL Execution Time Prediction, pp. 250–253)
- Predicts execution duration of unknown SQL queries using **SQL vectorization and template-based similarity** against historical execution logs **without collecting execution plans** (zero impact on DB performance; works for both OLTP and OLAP!).
- Requires GUC `log_statement = all` and `log_statement_stats = on`.
- Usage: `python main.py -m train -f data/train.csv` and `python main.py -m predict -f data/predict.csv`.

#### C. `Index-advisor` (3 Index Recommendation Functions, pp. 254–263)
1. **Single-Query Index Recommendation**:
   ```sql
   SELECT * FROM gs_index_advise('SELECT name, age, sex FROM t1 WHERE age >= 18 AND age < 35 AND sex = ''f'';');
   -- Supports ONLY a single SELECT statement on standard row-store tables!
   ```
2. **Virtual (Hypothetical) Index Recommendation**:
   - Simulates an index in the optimizer without physical creation time/space overhead:
   ```sql
   SELECT * FROM hypopg_create_index('CREATE INDEX ON bmsql_customer(c_w_id)');
   SET enable_hypo_index = on;               -- Default is off!
   EXPLAIN SELECT c_discount FROM bmsql_customer WHERE c_w_id = 10;
   -- Companion functions: hypopg_display_index(), hypopg_drop_index(oid), hypopg_reset_index(), hypopg_estimate_size(oid)
   ```
3. **Workload-Level Index Recommendation**:
   ```bash
   python index_advisor_workload.py 6001 postgres tpcc_log.txt --max_index_num 10 --multi_iter_mode
   ```
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![X-Tuner Deep Reinforcement Learning Parameter Optimization Loop (Official Reference: p. 246)](./assets/images/p3_h4s4_xtuner_drl.png)
*Figure: X-Tuner Deep Reinforcement Learning Parameter Optimization Loop (Official Reference: p. 246)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. DB4AI: `DeepSQL` & Native DB4AI Engine (pp. 264–267)
- **`DeepSQL`**: Encapsulates **60+ machine learning & graph algorithms** (Linear/Logistic Regression, Random Forest, KNN, K-Means, PCA, shortest path, graph diameter, Pearson correlation) into SQL statements (requires Python 2.7.12+ and `PL/Python`).
- **Native DB4AI Engine**: Integrates native AI operators and execution planning directly into the openGauss kernel with SQL-like syntax (**`CREATE MODEL ...`** and **`PREDICT BY ...`**), eliminating external Python/platform data transfers.
key_takeaways: X-Tuner runs in 3 modes: `recommend` (completes in seconds without DB restart), `train` (trains DRL model), and `tune` (uses DRL or global search algorithms).
SQLdiag predicts SQL execution time from historical logs using SQL vectorization and templates WITHOUT needing SQL execution plans.

Index-advisor provides 3 levels: `gs_index_advise('SELECT ...')` (single query), `hypopg_create_index(...)` with `SET enable_hypo_index = on` (virtual index), and `index_advisor_workload.py` (workload-level).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: After creating a virtual index with `hypopg_create_index()`, the optimizer will NOT use it in `EXPLAIN` unless you set `SET enable_hypo_index = on;` (default is `off`, Ch.03 p. 258)!

EXAM TRAP: `gs_index_advise()` supports ONLY a single `SELECT` statement and does NOT support column-store tables, views, materialized views, global temp tables, or encrypted databases (Ch.03 p. 255).

lecture.title: Logical Structure & Core Objects (Databases, Schemas, Tables, Views, Indexes, Transactions)
objectives: Navigate the logical hierarchy (Tablespace -> Database -> Schema -> Table -> Datafile Segment -> 8 KB Block)
Use `gsql` meta-commands (`\h`, `\c`, `\l`, `\dt`, `\d`, `\db`) and manage Schemas (`public`, `pg_temp`), Views, and Indexes
Contrast `READ COMMITTED` (statement-level snapshot, default) and `REPEATABLE READ` (transaction-level snapshot) isolation levels
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Logical Structure & `gsql` Meta-Commands (pp. 277–285)
- **Logical Hierarchy**:
  - **Tablespace**: Physical directory mapping; can hold files for multiple databases.
  - **Database**: Isolated collection of schemas and objects (default database: **`postgres`**; default templates: **`template0`**, **`template1`**).
  - **Schema**: Logical namespace container inside a database (cannot be nested). Every new database has a **`public`** schema by default. Creating a user via `CREATE USER` automatically creates a **schema with the same name** as the user!
  - **Table -> Datafile Segment (> 1 GB split) -> Block (8 KB default)**.
- **Essential `gsql` Meta-Commands (p. 285)**:
  - `\h [NAME]`: View SQL syntax help (e.g., `\h create user`).
  - `\l`: List all databases.
  - `\c dbname`: Switch/connect to `dbname`.
  - `\dt`: List all tables in the current schema/database.
  - `\d tablename`: Describe columns, types, and indexes of `tablename` (or system catalog).
  - `\db`: List all tablespaces.
  - `\q`: Quit `gsql`.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Tablespace, Database, Table, and Data Block Hierarchy (Official Reference: p. 277)](./assets/images/p3_h5s1_logical_arch.png)
*Figure: openGauss Tablespace, Database, Table, and Data Block Hierarchy (Official Reference: p. 277)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Core Objects: Indexes, Views & Schemas (pp. 288–292)
- **Indexes (pp. 288–289)**:
  - Recommended on: frequently queried columns, `JOIN` condition columns (composite index), `WHERE` filter/range columns, and `ORDER BY` / `GROUP BY` / `DISTINCT` columns.
  - Types: Single-column, Composite (`(col1, col2)`), Unique (`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`), Expression/Function-based (`ON table (expression)`), and Partial (`WHERE predicate`).
- **Views (`CREATE [TEMP] VIEW view_name AS query;`, p. 290)**:
  - A **virtual table**: only the view definition is stored in the database; actual data remains in the base tables.
- **Schemas (`CREATE SCHEMA`, pp. 291–292)**:
  - **Public Schema Security Rule**: All users have `USAGE` on `public` by default, but **only `SYSADMIN` and initial users** can create functions, aggregates, stored procedures, and synonyms in `public`, and **only the initial user** can create operators in `public`!
  - **Internal Schemas**: Schemas starting with **`pg_temp`** or **`pg_toast_temp`** are for internal temporary tables/TOAST — **never drop them**!

---

### 3. Transaction Isolation Levels in openGauss (p. 293)

| Isolation Level | Snapshot Timing | Visibility Behavior & Application Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`READ COMMITTED` (Default)** | **Statement-level snapshot** (new snapshot taken at the start of *each* `SELECT` statement) | Sees only data committed before the statement began (plus own uncommitted updates). Two consecutive `SELECT`s in the same transaction may see different data if another transaction commits in between. |
| **`REPEATABLE READ`** | **Transaction-level snapshot** (single snapshot taken at the start of the *first* statement in the transaction) | Repeated `SELECT` statements within the same transaction always see the exact same data snapshot. Applications must be prepared to retry transactions on serialization conflicts. |
key_takeaways: When `CREATE USER` is executed, openGauss automatically creates a schema with the same name as the user in the current database.
Schemas cannot be nested, and internal schemas starting with `pg_temp` or `pg_toast_temp` must never be dropped.
At `READ COMMITTED` (default), each statement takes a fresh snapshot; at `REPEATABLE READ`, the transaction uses the snapshot taken at the start of the transaction.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: A view is a virtual table — the database stores ONLY the view definition, NOT the view data (except materialized views).

EXAM TRAP: Even if an ordinary user is granted `CREATE` permission on the `public` schema, only `SYSADMIN`/initial users can create functions, aggregate functions, stored procedures, and synonyms in `public` (Ch.04 p. 291)!

lecture.title: Storage Engine Selection & Memory-Optimized Table (MOT)
objectives: Select the optimal storage engine (Row-store, Column-store, or MOT) based on workload characteristics
Explain MOT architecture, performance benchmarks (2.5x–4x throughput, 4.8M tpmC on 4-socket 256-core ARM, 3x–5.5x lower latency, 99% CPU utilization), and memory formula
Authorize `mot_server` (`GRANT USAGE ON FOREIGN SERVER`), create/drop MOTs (`CREATE/DROP FOREIGN TABLE`), and index MOTs (`CREATE INDEX` without `FOREIGN`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Storage Engine Selection Rules (pp. 295–301)

| Selection Factor | Choose Row-Store (`ORIENTATION = ROW`) | Choose Column-Store (`ORIENTATION = COLUMN`) | Choose MOT (Memory-Optimized Table) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Update / Insert Pattern** | Frequent updates; frequent small inserts | Rarely updated; **large batch inserts** | Mission-critical, ultra-low-latency OLTP |
| **Column Width & Projection** | Narrow tables or queries reading most columns | Wide tables where queries touch **< 50% of columns** | All data **AND** indexes fit in RAM |
| **Query Pattern** | Index point queries returning a few rows | Statistical aggregation (`SUM`, `AVG`, `GROUP BY`) & ad-hoc scans | High-concurrency, high-contention OLTP |
| **Compression** | Moderate compression | **High compression ratio** (trades higher CPU usage for smaller I/O) | In-memory NUMA-aware row store |
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Row-Store Table Sequential Tuple Disk Layout (Official Reference: p. 296)](./assets/images/p3_h5s2_rowstore_table.png)
*Figure: Row-Store Table Sequential Tuple Disk Layout (Official Reference: p. 296)*

![Column-Store Table Columnar Compression Layout (Official Reference: p. 298)](./assets/images/p3_h5s2_columnstore_table.png)
*Figure: Column-Store Table Columnar Compression Layout (Official Reference: p. 298)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Memory-Optimized Table (MOT) Architecture & Benchmarks (pp. 302–304)
- **What is MOT?**: Production-grade transactional **in-memory row-store engine** integrated with openGauss via the **Foreign Data Wrapper (`FDW`)** mechanism (`mot_server`), storing **both data and indexes entirely in memory**.
- **Core Technical Pillars**:
  - **NUMA-aware memory management** + **Lock-free concurrency control & indexing** + **Native query compilation (JIT/LLVM)** + full **ACID** support (WAL logging, Checkpoints, Recovery; supports `READ COMMITTED` and `REPEATABLE READ`).
  - *Prerequisite*: Set `enable_incremental_checkpoint = off` in `postgresql.conf` before creating MOT tables.
- **Official Huawei TaiShan (ARM/Kunpeng) TPC-C Benchmarks (p. 304)**:
  - **Throughput**: **2.5x to 4x** higher than disk tables (**2.5x** gain on 2-socket servers; **4.8 million tpmC** on 4-socket 256-core Arm servers).
  - **Latency**: Reduces transaction latency by **3x to 5.5x**.
  - **Resource Utilization**: Reaches **99% CPU utilization** on 4-socket servers under high load and high contention.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![openGauss Dual Storage Architecture: Disk Engine vs Memory-Optimized Table (MOT) (Official Reference: p. 303)](./assets/images/p3_h5s2_dual_storage_mot.png)
*Figure: openGauss Dual Storage Architecture: Disk Engine vs Memory-Optimized Table (MOT) (Official Reference: p. 303)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. MOT Memory Formula & SQL Syntax (p. 305)
- **Mandatory Memory Formula**:
  $$(max\_mot\_global\_memory + max\_mot\_local\_memory) + 2 GB < max\_process\_memory$$
  - **Global memory**: Long-term memory shared across all CPU cores storing all MOT table data and indexes.
  - **Local memory**: Short-term session memory used to handle private transaction data changes until commit.
- **MOT SQL Syntax (FDW Mechanism)**:
  ```sql
  -- 1. Grant user permission to use mot_server (run once per user)
  GRANT USAGE ON FOREIGN SERVER mot_server TO jack;
  -- 2. Create an MOT (uses FOREIGN keyword!)
  CREATE FOREIGN TABLE test(x INT) SERVER mot_server;
  -- 3. Create an index on MOT (DO NOT use FOREIGN keyword here!)
  CREATE INDEX text_index1 ON test(x);
  -- 4. Drop an MOT (uses FOREIGN keyword!)
  DROP FOREIGN TABLE test;
  ```
  - *Converting a disk table to MOT*: Use `gs_dump` to dump the disk table data, replace `CREATE TABLE` with `CREATE FOREIGN TABLE`, and use `gs_restore` / `gsql` to load data into the MOT.
key_takeaways: MOT stores all data and indexes in memory using lock-free algorithms and NUMA-aware design, achieving 2.5x–4x higher throughput (4.8M tpmC on 4-socket 256-core ARM) and 3x–5.5x lower latency.
MOT memory configuration must satisfy `(max_mot_global_memory + max_mot_local_memory) + 2 GB < max_process_memory`.

MOT is integrated via FDW (`GRANT USAGE ON FOREIGN SERVER mot_server TO <user>;`): use `CREATE FOREIGN TABLE` and `DROP FOREIGN TABLE`, but do NOT use the `FOREIGN` keyword in `CREATE INDEX` or `DROP INDEX`!
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: When creating or dropping an index on an MOT, do NOT include the `FOREIGN` keyword (`CREATE INDEX idx ON test(x);`, NOT `CREATE FOREIGN INDEX`)! `FOREIGN` is used only in `CREATE FOREIGN TABLE` and `DROP FOREIGN TABLE` (Ch.04 p. 305).
EXAM TRAP: If a query touches less than 50% of the total columns in a wide table for analytical aggregation, choose a Column-Store table (Ch.04 p. 301).

lecture.title: Tablespaces, Users, Roles & Permission Management
objectives: Create, inspect, size, rename, and drop Tablespaces (`CREATE TABLESPACE ... RELATIVE LOCATION`, `PG_TABLESPACE_SIZE`, `\db`, 90% read-only threshold)
Explain why Users and Roles are NOT fully equivalent (Ch.04 Quiz Q1: False! Users have `LOGIN` by default, Roles do not)
Manage Users/Roles (`CREATE/ALTER/DROP USER/ROLE`), Account Validity (`VALID BEGIN ... VALID UNTIL`), Locking (`ACCOUNT LOCK/UNLOCK`), and Private Users (`WITH INDEPENDENT`)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Tablespace Management & 90% Read-Only Threshold (pp. 307–310)
- **Why Use Tablespaces?**:
  1. Expand storage onto other disk partitions when the initial volume is full.
  2. Separate hot objects (e.g., frequently accessed indexes on fast SSDs) from cold archived tables (on slower disks).
  3. **90% Read-Only Protection Rule (p. 307)**: If the disk usage where a tablespace resides reaches **90%**, openGauss **automatically switches the database to read-only mode**! It switches back to read/write mode once disk usage drops below 90%.
- **Tablespace SQL Operations (pp. 308–310)**:
  ```sql
  -- 1. Create tablespace (relative to instance data directory; must be an empty r/w directory)
  CREATE TABLESPACE fastspace RELATIVE LOCATION 'tablespace/tablespace_1';
  -- 2. Grant CREATE permission on tablespace
  GRANT CREATE ON TABLESPACE fastspace TO jack;
  -- 3. Create table in tablespace (or SET default_tablespace = 'fastspace';)
  CREATE TABLE foo(i INT) TABLESPACE fastspace;
  -- 4. Inspect tablespaces & check size
  \db
  SELECT * FROM pg_tablespace;
  SELECT PG_TABLESPACE_SIZE('fastspace');
  -- 5. Rename & drop tablespace (owner or sysadmin only; must be empty)
  ALTER TABLESPACE fastspace RENAME TO fspace;
  DROP TABLESPACE fspace;
  ```

---

### 2. Users vs. Roles (`pg_authid`, `PUBLIC`, Ch.04 Quiz Q1!)
- **User vs. Role Distinction (pp. 312–315, 324, 346)**:
  - **User**: An entity/individual that connects to the database (`rolcanlogin = true` / **`LOGIN` privilege enabled by default**).
  - **Role**: A carrier of permission sets representing behavioral constraints (**does NOT have `LOGIN` permission by default**).
  - **CRITICAL EXAM FACT (Ch.04 Quiz Q1: False!)**: Although `CREATE USER` and `CREATE ROLE` share the same syntax in openGauss, **users and roles are NOT fully equivalent** because `CREATE USER` grants `LOGIN` by default whereas `CREATE ROLE` does not (`NOLOGIN` by default)!
- **Implicit `PUBLIC` Group (p. 313)**: All new users and roles implicitly inherit permissions granted to `PUBLIC` (use `GRANT/REVOKE ... TO/FROM PUBLIC` to manage).
- **System Catalog & Views (p. 317, 324)**: User/role attributes are stored in the cluster-wide system catalog **`pg_authid`** (accessible **only to `SYSADMIN`**) and exposed via **`pg_user`** and **`pg_roles`** views.

---

### 3. Account Validity, Manual Lock/Unlock & Private (`INDEPENDENT`) Users (pp. 318–321)
- **Dropping Users (`DROP USER`, p. 318)**: Uses **`RESTRICT` by default** — if the user owns database objects, `DROP USER` fails unless **`CASCADE`** is specified (`DROP USER IF EXISTS joe CASCADE;`).
- **Setting Account Validity Period (p. 319)**:
  ```sql
  CREATE USER joe WITH PASSWORD 'Bigdata@123'
      VALID BEGIN '2015-10-10 08:00:00' VALID UNTIL '2016-10-10 08:00:00';
  ALTER USER joe WITH VALID BEGIN '2016-11-10 08:00:00' VALID UNTIL '2017-11-10 08:00:00';
  ```
- **Manually Locking and Unlocking Accounts (p. 320)**:
  ```sql
  ALTER USER user_read ACCOUNT LOCK;
  ALTER USER user_read ACCOUNT UNLOCK;
  ```
- **Private User (`WITH INDEPENDENT`, p. 321)**:
  ```sql
  CREATE USER user_independent WITH INDEPENDENT IDENTIFIED BY '1234@abc';
  ```
  - Isolates DBA control permissions from data access permissions in non-separation-of-duties mode: **DBAs (`SYSADMIN`) can manage (`DROP`, `ALTER`, `TRUNCATE`) objects of an `INDEPENDENT` user, but CANNOT access (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `COPY`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `ALTER OWNER`) their data without explicit authorization from that user!**
key_takeaways: Users and roles have the same syntax in openGauss, but they are NOT fully equivalent (Ch.04 Quiz Q1: False) because `CREATE USER` includes `LOGIN` by default whereas `CREATE ROLE` does not.
If the disk hosting a tablespace reaches 90% usage, openGauss automatically switches to read-only mode.

For a Private User (`CREATE USER ... WITH INDEPENDENT`), DBAs can manage (`DROP`, `ALTER`, `TRUNCATE`) their objects but cannot access (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `COPY`) their data without authorization.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.04 Quiz Q1): '(True or False) Users and roles have the same syntax in the openGauss database. Therefore, they are fully equivalent.' -> B. False!
EXAM TRAP: If a user owns database objects, `DROP USER username;` fails because `RESTRICT` is the default; you must use `DROP USER username CASCADE;` (Ch.04 p. 318).

objectives: Identify key openGauss System Catalogs (`PG_CLASS`, `PG_ATTRIBUTE`, `PG_AUTHID`, `PG_DATABASE`, `PG_INDEX`, `PG_NAMESPACE`, `PG_PARTITION`) and Views (`PG_STAT_ACTIVITY`, `PG_SETTINGS`, `PG_LOCKS`)

lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Essential System Catalogs & System Views (pp. 323–328)

| System Catalog (`PG_*`) | Stored Metadata | System View | Displayed Information |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`PG_DATABASE`** | Available databases | **`PG_STAT_ACTIVITY`** | Current user sessions and running queries |
| **`PG_CLASS`** | Tables, indexes, views, sequences & relationships | **`PG_SETTINGS`** | Runtime GUC parameters of the database |
| **`PG_ATTRIBUTE`** | Table columns | **`PG_LOCKS`** | Locks held by open transactions |
| **`PG_AUTHID`** | Roles & users (`rolcanlogin`; `SYSADMIN` only) | **`PG_ROLES` / `PG_USER`** | Role and user information |
| **`PG_CONSTRAINT`** | Check, PK, Unique, and FK constraints | **`PG_STATS`** | Single-column statistics from `pg_statistic` |
| **`PG_INDEX`** | Index metadata (rest in `PG_CLASS`) | **`GS_SQL_COUNT`** | Counts of `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE INTO` |
| **`PG_NAMESPACE`** | Schemas (namespaces) | **`GS_AUDITING` / `GS_MASKING` / `GS_LABELS`** | Audit info, masking policies, and resource labels (`SYSADMIN`/`POLADMIN`) |
| **`PG_PARTITION`** | Partitioned tables, table partitions, index partitions | **`PLAN_TABLE`** | Session-level execution plan info from `EXPLAIN PLAN` |
| **`PG_DEPEND` / `PG_PROC` / `PG_JOB`** | Object dependencies (`CASCADE`/`RESTRICT`), functions/procedures, scheduled jobs | **`GS_WLM_USER_RESOURCE_HISTORY`** | Reserved catalog for user resource usage history |

---

### 2. Data Import & Export: `INSERT`, `COPY`, and `\copy` (pp. 330–333, Ch.04 Quiz Q2!)
1. **`INSERT`**: Simplest way to add data via client or JDBC/ODBC; suitable for **small data volume and low concurrency**.
2. **SQL `COPY` (`COPY FROM` / `COPY TO`, server-side file I/O) & JDBC `CopyManager` (`org.postgresql.copy.CopyManager`)**:
   - Applies **only to tables, NOT views**.
   - **Exporting Partial Table Data (Exact Ch.04 Quiz Q2: C!)**:
     ```sql
     COPY t1 FROM '/data/input/t1.txt' DELIMITER '^';
     COPY t1 TO '/data/input/t1_output.txt' DELIMITER '^';
     -- Export partial data using a conditional SELECT query:
     COPY (SELECT * FROM student WHERE age > 20) TO '/data/input/student_part.txt' DELIMITER '^';
     ```
3. **`gsql` `\copy` Meta-Command (Client-side file I/O, p. 333)**:
   - Unlike SQL `COPY` (which reads/writes files on the **database server**), `\copy` reads/writes files on the **local `gsql` client host** using the local OS user's file permissions!
   - Default delimiters: **Tab** in `TEXT` format, **Comma (`,`)** in `CSV` format, none in `FIXED` format.

---

### 3. `gs_dump`, `gs_dumpall`, `gs_restore`, `VACUUM FULL` & `ANALYZE` (pp. 334–345)
- **`gs_dump` Key Flags (p. 335)**:
  - `-U <user>`, `-W <pass>`, `-p <port>`, `-f <file>`, `-F p|c|d|t` (format), **`-n <schema>`** (include schema), **`-t <schema.table>`** (include table), **`-T <schema.table>`** (exclude table; if both `-t` and `-T` are given, exports objects in `-t` that are not in `-T`).
  - **Exporting without direct permission (p. 340)**: Use **`--role <rolename> --rolepassword <pass>`** to assume a role that has export privileges!
- **`gs_restore` Key Flags (pp. 341–343)**:
  - Imports `.tar` (`t`), custom (`c`), or directory (`d`) archives exported by `gs_dump`.
  - **`-d <dbname>`** (target DB), **`-c`** (clean/drop existing objects before recreating), **`-e`** (exit immediately on SQL error), **`-s`** (import **schema/object definitions only**, no data).
- **Post-Import Maintenance (pp. 344–345)**:
  - **`VACUUM FULL tablename;`**: Reclaims disk page fragments left by mass updates/deletions and **returns free space to the OS** (run **before** `ANALYZE`).
  - **`ANALYZE tablename;`**: Updates `PG_STATISTIC` so the CBO generates optimal query plans after data import.
key_takeaways: To export partial data from a table (e.g., rows matching a condition), use `COPY (SELECT ... WHERE ...) TO '/path/file'` (Ch.04 Quiz Q2: C). `gs_dump` and `gs_dumpall` export whole tables/databases, not conditional subsets.
SQL `COPY` reads/writes files on the database server, whereas the `gsql` meta-command `\copy` reads/writes files on the local client machine.
After bulk imports/updates/deletes, run `VACUUM FULL <table_name>;` (to reclaim disk page fragments to the OS) followed by `ANALYZE <table_name>;` (to update `PG_STATISTIC`).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.04 Quiz Q2): 'Which of the following commands can be used to export partial data from the student table?' -> C. `copy` Conditional statement (`COPY (SELECT ...) TO ...`)!
EXAM TRAP: In `gs_restore`, `-s` imports ONLY object definitions (schemas/tables without data), `-c` drops existing objects before recreating them, and `-e` exits immediately if an error occurs.

lecture.title: SQL Classification (DDL, DML, DCL, DQL) & Data Types
objectives: Classify SQL commands into DDL (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`), DML (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`), DCL (`COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `LOCK TABLE`), and DQL (`SELECT`)
Memorize exact storage byte sizes for Integer, Serial, Floating-Point, Arbitrary-Precision, Character, Date/Time, Binary, and Boolean types
Avoid the classic exam traps on `BIGINT` (8 bytes, NOT 4 bytes — Ch.05 Quiz!) and `CLOB` (large `TEXT` object — Ch.05 Quiz!)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Four-Way SQL Statement Classification (pp. 358–359, Ch.05 Quizzes!)

| Category | Full Name | Core SQL Statements in openGauss |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **DDL** | **Data Definition Language** | **`CREATE`**, **`ALTER`**, **`DROP`**, **`TRUNCATE TABLE`** (defines/modifies databases, tablespaces, tables, indexes, views, sequences, users, roles, functions) — *Ch.05 p. 446 Quiz Q2: C!* |
| **DML** | **Data Manipulation Language** | **`INSERT`**, **`UPDATE`**, **`DELETE`** (plus `LOAD`, `DUMP`, `EXPLAIN PLAN`) — *Ch.05 p. 405 Quiz Q2: B!* |
| **DCL** | **Data Control Language** | **`COMMIT`**, **`ROLLBACK`**, **`GRANT`**, **`REVOKE`**, **`LOCK TABLE`**, **`SHUTDOWN`** |
| **DQL** | **Data Query Language** | **`SELECT`** (and set combinations of multiple `SELECT` statements) |

---

### 2. Numeric, Character, Date/Time, Binary & Boolean Data Types (pp. 361–372)

| Type Family | Data Type | Storage Space | Key Exam Notes & Aliases |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Integers** | **`TINYINT` (`INT1`)** | **1 byte** | Whole numbers without decimals |
| | **`SMALLINT` (`INT2`)** | **2 bytes** | Used when range is guaranteed small |
| | **`INTEGER` (`INT4` / `BINARY_INTEGER`)** | **4 bytes** | Best balance of range, size, and speed |
| | **`BIGINT` (`INT8`)** | **8 bytes** | **EXAM TRAP (p. 372 Q1)**: Occupies **8 bytes**, **NOT 4 bytes**! |
| **Serial (Auto-Inc)** | `SMALLSERIAL` / `SERIAL` / `BIGSERIAL` | **2 / 4 / 8 bytes** | Not true types; creates integer col + sequence + `NOT NULL`. Cannot be added via `ALTER TABLE` or used in temp tables. |
| **Arbitrary Precision** | `NUMERIC(p,s)` / `DECIMAL(p,s)` / `NUMBER(p,s)` / `DEC(p,s)` | **2 bytes per 4 decimal digits + 8-byte overhead** | `p` (precision) in `[1, 1000]`, `s` (scale) in `[0, p]` |
| **Floating-Point** | `REAL` (`FLOAT4`) | **4 bytes** | Single-precision inexact float |
| | `DOUBLE PRECISION` (`FLOAT8` / `BINARY_DOUBLE`) | **8 bytes** | Double-precision inexact float (`FLOAT(p)` is 4 or 8B for p \in [1,53]) |
| **Character** | `CHAR(n)` / `CHARACTER(n)` / `NCHAR(n)` | Up to **10 MB** | Fixed-length, blank-padded (default n=1). ASCII = 1B/char; Unicode = 2B/char. |
| | `VARCHAR(n)` / `VARCHAR2(n)` / `NVARCHAR2(n)` | Up to **10 MB** | Variable-length string without blank padding |
| | **`TEXT` / `CLOB`** | Up to **1 GB – 1 byte** | **`CLOB` is an alias of `TEXT` used to store large text objects (p. 372 Q2: True!)** |
| **Date / Time** | `DATE` | **4 bytes** | Date and time |
| | `TIME [WITHOUT TIME ZONE]` / `TIMESTAMP` / `TIMESTAMPTZ` / `SMALLDATETIME` | **8 bytes** | `SMALLDATETIME` precision is 1 minute (30s–60s rounds up to 1 min!) |
| | `TIME WITH TIME ZONE` / `INTERVAL [FIELDS]` | **12 bytes** | `INTERVAL DAY(l) TO SECOND(p)` occupies **16 bytes** |
| **Binary & Boolean** | `BYTEA` / `RAW` / `BLOB` | Up to **1 GB – 8203 B** | `BOOLEAN` occupies **1 byte** (`TRUE`/`1` or `FALSE`/`0`) |
key_takeaways: `TINYINT` = 1 byte, `SMALLINT` = 2 bytes, `INTEGER` (`BINARY_INTEGER`) = 4 bytes, and `BIGINT` = 8 bytes (Ch.05 p. 372 Quiz Q1: `BIGINT occupies four bytes` is FALSE!).
`CLOB` is an alias of `TEXT` (up to 1 GB minus 1 byte) used to store large character/text objects (Ch.05 p. 372 Quiz Q2: TRUE!).
`INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` are DML commands (p. 405 Quiz Q2), whereas `CREATE, DROP, ALTER` are DDL commands (p. 446 Quiz Q2).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.05 p. 372 Quiz Q1): '(True or false) BIGINT occupies four bytes.' -> B. False! `BIGINT` (`INT8`) occupies EIGHT (8) bytes (`INTEGER`/`INT4` occupies 4 bytes).
EXAM TRAP (Ch.05 p. 372 Quiz Q2): '(True or false) CLOB is used to store large object data of the TEXT type.' -> A. True!

objectives: Write `SELECT` queries with column/table aliases (`AS` or space) and `WHERE` conditions (`Position = 'Engineer' AND Salary > 6000`, `BETWEEN ... AND ...`)
Sort results with `ORDER BY` using column names, 1-based column positions (`ORDER BY 2 DESC, 3 ASC` — Ch.05 Quiz!), or expressions, plus `NULLS FIRST | LAST`
Paginate queries using `LIMIT count OFFSET start`, `OFFSET start LIMIT count`, and `LIMIT offset, count`
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Relational Operations & Conditional Filtering (`WHERE`, pp. 374–382, 394)
- **3 Relational Algebra Operations in `SELECT` (p. 374)**:
  1. **`SELECT` (Selection)**: Filters rows (tuples) that satisfy a condition.
  2. **`PROJECT` (Projection)**: Selects specific columns (attributes) and filters out others.
  3. **`JOIN`**: Combines rows from multiple tables.
- **Conditional Query Rules (`WHERE`, pp. 380–382, Ch.05 p. 394 Quizzes!)**:
  - **String & Date Literals**: Single quotation marks (`'...'`) are optional for numbers but **mandatory for character strings and dates**!
    - **Ch.05 p. 394 Quiz Q1**: Searching for records whose position is an engineer and salary > 6000 is **`Position = 'Engineer' AND Salary > 6000`** (Option D — `'Engineer'` must be in single quotes and joined with `AND`!).
  - **Range Predicate (`BETWEEN ... AND ...`)**: Inclusive on both bounds!
    - **Ch.05 p. 394 Quiz Q2**: **`age BETWEEN 20 AND 30`** is strictly equivalent to **`age >= 20 AND age <= 30`** (Option A!).
  - **Logical Operator Precedence & Three-Valued Logic (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, `NULL`)**:
    - Priority order: **`NOT` > `AND` > `OR`**.
    - Truth table with `NULL` (Unknown):
      - **`TRUE OR NULL` -> `TRUE`**; **`FALSE OR NULL` -> `NULL`**.
      - **`FALSE AND NULL` -> `FALSE`**; **`TRUE AND NULL` -> `NULL`**.
      - **`NOT NULL` -> `NULL`**.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![Relational Operations: SELECT (Rows), PROJECT (Columns), JOIN (Merge) (Official Reference: p. 374)](./assets/images/p3_h6s2_sql_ops_visual.png)
*Figure: Relational Operations: SELECT (Rows), PROJECT (Columns), JOIN (Merge) (Official Reference: p. 374)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Data Sorting (`ORDER BY`, pp. 390–391, 395)
```sql
ORDER BY { column_name | number | expression } [ ASC | DESC ] [ NULLS FIRST | NULLS LAST ] [, ...]
```
- **Default Order**: **`ASC`** (ascending) is the default when neither `ASC` nor `DESC` is specified!
- **Sorting by Column Position (`number`)**: `1` refers to the 1st column in the `SELECT` list, `2` refers to the 2nd column, etc.
  - **Ch.05 p. 395 Quiz Q3 (Answer: AC!)**: To query `name, age, score` from `student` sorted by `age` descending and then `score` ascending:
    - **Option A**: `SELECT name, age, score FROM student order by age desc, score;` (valid because `score` defaults to `ASC`!)
    - **Option C**: `SELECT name, age, score FROM student order by 2 desc, 3 asc;` (valid because `2` is `age` and `3` is `score`!)
- **Default `NULL` Placement (p. 390)**:
  - For **`ASC`**, **`NULLS FIRST`** is the default in openGauss (per slide 38, p. 390).
  - For **`DESC`**, **`NULLS LAST`** is the default.

---

### 3. Data Limit & Pagination (`LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, pp. 392–393)
- **`LIMIT count`**: Maximum number of rows to return.
- **`OFFSET start`**: Number of initial rows to skip before returning rows.
- **Three Equivalent Syntax Forms in openGauss (p. 392)**:
  - **`LIMIT 5, 20`** \equiv **`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 5`** \equiv **`OFFSET 5 LIMIT 20`**
  - All three mean: **skip the first 5 rows, and return at most 20 rows**!
key_takeaways: String literals in `WHERE` must be enclosed in single quotes (`Position = 'Engineer' AND Salary > 6000`), and `age BETWEEN 20 AND 30` is equivalent to `age >= 20 AND age <= 30` (Ch.05 p. 394 Q1 & Q2).

In `ORDER BY`, `ASC` is the default direction, and you can reference `SELECT` columns by their 1-based position (`ORDER BY 2 DESC, 3 ASC` is equivalent to `ORDER BY age DESC, score` for `SELECT name, age, score` — Ch.05 p. 395 Q3: AC).
`LIMIT 5, 20`, `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 5`, and `OFFSET 5 LIMIT 20` are all equivalent and output 20 rows after skipping 5 rows.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.05 p. 395 Quiz Q3): Both `SELECT name, age, score FROM student order by age desc, score;` (A) and `SELECT name, age, score FROM student order by 2 desc, 3 asc;` (C) are correct! Don't forget that omitting `ASC` after `score` defaults to ascending order.

EXAM TRAP: In `LIMIT 5, 20` (comma syntax), the FIRST number (`5`) is the offset (rows skipped) and the SECOND number (`20`) is the row count, whereas in `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 5`, `20` is the count and `5` is the offset!

lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Cartesian Product & Join Basics (pp. 383–384)
- **Cartesian Product (Direct Product, X \× Y, p. 383)**:
  - If table X has **I tuples (rows)** and **N attributes (columns)**, and table Y has **J tuples** and **M attributes**, then `SELECT * FROM X, Y;` (a join without any `WHERE` or `ON` join condition) produces:
    - **I \× J tuples (rows)** (e.g., 4 rows in A \× 5 rows in B = **20 rows**).
    - **N + M attributes (columns)**.
- **Table References in `FROM`**: Can be ordinary tables, views, or subqueries (`(SELECT ...) AS alias`).
- **Note on `(+)` Outer Join Operator (p. 384)**: openGauss supports Oracle's `(+)` operator in `WHERE` clauses to convert a join into an outer join, **but it is NOT recommended** because it is not standard SQL syntax.

---

### 2. Inner Join vs. Outer Joins (`LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `FULL`, pp. 385–389)

| Join Type | Syntax (`OUTER` / `INNER` keyword is optional) | Returned Rows & `NULL` Padding Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Inner Join** | `A [INNER] JOIN B ON A.id = B.id` | Returns **only** rows that satisfy the join condition in **both** tables. |
| **Left Outer Join** | `A LEFT [OUTER] JOIN B ON A.id = B.id` | Driven by the **left table (`A`)**: returns all rows from `A` + matched data from `B`. Unmatched columns from `B` are filled with **`NULL`**. |
| **Right Outer Join** | `A RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN B ON A.id = B.id` | Driven by the **right table (`B`)**: returns all rows from `B` + matched data from `A`. Unmatched columns from `A` are filled with **`NULL`**. |
| **Full Outer Join** | `A FULL [OUTER] JOIN B ON A.id = B.id` | Returns all matched rows **plus** unmatched rows from `A` (padded with `NULL` on the right) **and** unmatched rows from `B` (padded with `NULL` on the left). |

---

### 3. Official Walkthrough: `education e` (`staff_id` 11, 12, 13) \\bowtie `training t` (`staff_id` 10, 11, 12) (pp. 387–389)
- **`education e`**: `(11, 'master')`, `(12, 'doctor')`, `(13, 'scholar')`
- **`training t`**: `(10, 90)`, `(11, 92)`, `(12, 95)`
  - **`INNER JOIN`**: Returns only `11` and `12` (2 rows).
  - **`e LEFT JOIN t`**: Returns `11` (`92`), `12` (`95`), and `13` (`score = NULL`) (3 rows).
  - **`e RIGHT JOIN t`**: Returns `NULL` (`staff_id` from `e` is `NULL`, `score = 90`), `11` (`92`), and `12` (`95`) (3 rows).
  - **`e FULL JOIN t`**: Returns `11`, `12`, `13` (`score = NULL`), and `NULL` (`score = 90`) (4 rows).

![Left Outer Join Row Matching Visual Example (Official Reference: p. 387)](./assets/images/p3_h6s3_left_outer_join.png)

![Right Outer Join Row Matching Visual Example (Official Reference: p. 388)](./assets/images/p3_h6s3_right_outer_join.png)

![Full Outer Join Row Matching Visual Example (Official Reference: p. 389)](./assets/images/p3_h6s3_full_outer_join.png)

key_takeaways: A Cartesian product between table X (I rows, N columns) and table Y (J rows, M columns) produces I * J rows and N + M columns.
`LEFT JOIN` preserves all rows from the left table (padding right columns with `NULL`), `RIGHT JOIN` preserves all rows from the right table, and `FULL JOIN` preserves unmatched rows from both sides.
In `LEFT JOIN`, `ON` clause conditions determine row matching (driving `NULL` extension), whereas outer `WHERE` conditions filter the resulting joined rows afterwards.

Because the `SELECT` list projected `e.staff_id` (from the left table), which has no match for `10`!

lecture.title: DML Statements — `INSERT`, `UPDATE` & `DELETE`
objectives: Master the 3 forms of `INSERT` (`INSERT ... VALUES`, `INSERT ... SELECT`, and `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` / `INSERT IGNORE`)
Write `UPDATE table SET col = expr [WHERE condition]` statements (`UPDATE STAFFS SET AGE = AGE + 5` — Ch.05 Quiz Q1!)
Write `DELETE FROM table [WHERE condition]` statements (`DELETE FROM student WHERE cid = 6;` — Ch.05 Quiz Q3!) and know column-store DML limitations
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Inserting Data (`INSERT`, pp. 397–399)
openGauss supports **three `INSERT` syntax patterns**:
1. **Insert explicit row values**:
   ```sql
   INSERT INTO bank_card(b_number, b_type, b_c_id) VALUES ('6222021302020000001', 'Credit Card', 1);
   ```
2. **Insert from a query (`INSERT ... SELECT`)**:
   ```sql
   INSERT INTO bank_card1 SELECT * FROM bank_card;
   -- Number of columns in SELECT list must match the target columns!
   ```
3. **Upsert on primary/unique key conflict (`ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` vs. `IGNORE`)**:
   ```sql
   INSERT INTO bank_card VALUES ('6222021302020000001', 'Credit Card', 1)
       ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE b_type = 'Savings Card';
   ```
   - **`IGNORE`** (`INSERT IGNORE INTO ...`): Silently ignores rows that cause duplicate key errors (**cannot** be used together with `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`!).
   - **Permissions**:
     - `RETURNING` clause requires `SELECT` permission on the table.
     - `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` requires `INSERT`, `SELECT`, and `UPDATE` on the table plus `SELECT` on the unique/primary key index.
   - **Record Size Limit (p. 397)**: Data size of a single inserted record must be **< 64,000 bytes** in standard row-store insert precautions.

---

### 2. Updating Data (`UPDATE`, pp. 400–401, Ch.05 p. 405 Quiz Q1!)
```sql
UPDATE table_reference SET col_name = expression [, ...] [ WHERE condition ];
```
- **Official Exam Question (Ch.05 p. 405 Quiz Q1: C!)**:
  - To increase the value of the `AGE` column in the `STAFFS` table by 5 years:
    ```sql
    UPDATE STAFFS SET AGE = AGE + 5;
    ```
  - *(Why are A, B, D wrong? Because SQL `UPDATE` uses `UPDATE <table> SET <col> = <expr>`, NEVER `WITH`!)*
- **Column-Store `UPDATE` Precautions (p. 400)**:
  - `RETURNING` clause is **not supported** for column-store tables.
  - Memory/space holding old records in a column-store table is **not automatically recycled** after `UPDATE` — you must run **`VACUUM FULL table_name;`** to reclaim it.
  - `UPDATE` is **not supported** on column-store replication tables.

---

### 3. Deleting Data (`DELETE`, pp. 402–404, Ch.05 p. 406 Quiz Q3!)
```sql
DELETE FROM [schema_name.]table_name [ WHERE condition ];
```
- **Official Exam Question (Ch.05 p. 406 Quiz Q3: A!)**:
  - To delete records for all students whose class ID (`cid`) is `6` from the `student` table:
    ```sql
    DELETE FROM student WHERE cid = 6;
    ```
  - **CRITICAL SYNTAX TRAP**: Never put `*` after `DELETE` (`DELETE * FROM ...` is a syntax error!), and use `WHERE` (not `ON`) for the filter condition!
  - If the `WHERE` clause is omitted (`DELETE FROM student;`), **all rows in the table are deleted**, leaving the empty table structure intact.
key_takeaways: To increment `AGE` by 5 in `STAFFS`, use `UPDATE STAFFS SET AGE = AGE + 5;` (Ch.05 p. 405 Quiz Q1: C).
To delete rows where `cid = 6` from `student`, use `DELETE FROM student WHERE cid = 6;` — there is NO `*` between `DELETE` and `FROM`, and the filter uses `WHERE`, not `ON` (Ch.05 p. 406 Quiz Q3: A).
`INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` updates specified columns when a primary/unique key conflict occurs, and cannot be combined with `INSERT IGNORE`.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.05 p. 406 Quiz Q3): `DELETE * FROM student WHERE cid = 6;` (B) is INVALID SQL! `DELETE` deletes entire rows, so `*` is never used after `DELETE`. The correct statement is `DELETE FROM student WHERE cid = 6;` (A).
EXAM TRAP: After updating rows in a column-store table, old record space is not recycled automatically; you must run `VACUUM FULL table_name;` (Ch.05 p. 400).

objectives: Create, replace, and drop Views (`CREATE OR REPLACE [TEMP] VIEW`, `DROP VIEW ... CASCADE | RESTRICT`)

Master the default `MINVALUE`/`MAXVALUE`/`START WITH` rules for ascending vs. descending sequences (Ch.05 p. 447 Quiz Q3: BD!)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Defining Views (`CREATE [OR REPLACE] VIEW`, `DROP VIEW`, pp. 438–440)
- **3 Core Benefits of Views (p. 438)**:
  1. **Simplify complex queries**: Encapsulate frequently used multi-table joins/filters into a single virtual table (`SELECT * FROM view_name;`).
  2. **Enhance security**: Expose only non-sensitive columns/rows while hiding sensitive columns in the base table.
  3. **Ensure logical data independence**: Decouple application queries from physical base table restructuring.
- **Syntax**:
  ```sql
  CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW privilege_view AS SELECT b_number, b_type FROM bank_card;
  SELECT * FROM privilege_view;
  \d privilege_view
  DROP VIEW IF EXISTS privilege_view RESTRICT; -- RESTRICT is default; CASCADE drops dependent views
  ```

---

### 2. Defining Sequences (`CREATE / ALTER / DROP SEQUENCE`, pp. 441–445)
A **sequence** is a special single-row object that generates arithmetic progressions (typically used for auto-incrementing primary keys via `DEFAULT nextval('seq_name')`):
```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE name
    [ INCREMENT [ BY ] increment ]
    [ MINVALUE minvalue | NO MINVALUE | NOMINVALUE ]
    [ MAXVALUE maxvalue | NO MAXVALUE | NOMAXVALUE ]
    [ START [ WITH ] start ]
    [ CACHE cache ]
    [ [ NO ] CYCLE | NOCYCLE ]
    [ OWNED BY { table_name.column_name | NONE } ];
```

---

### 3. Ascending vs. Descending Sequence Default Rules (p. 442, Ch.05 p. 447 Quiz Q3: BD!)
This table is **one of the highest-yield exam topics in HCIA-openGauss V2.0**:

| Parameter | Ascending Sequence (`INCREMENT > 0`, Default `+1`) | Descending (Decremental) Sequence (`INCREMENT < 0`, e.g., `-4`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Default `MINVALUE`** | **`1`** | **`-2^63 - 1`** (minimum 64-bit signed integer) |
| **Default `MAXVALUE`** | **`2^63 - 1`** (maximum 64-bit signed integer) | **`-1`** (**CRITICAL!** If `MAXVALUE` is omitted on a negative-increment sequence, `MAXVALUE` defaults to **`-1`**!) |
| **Default `START WITH`** | **`minvalue`** | **`maxvalue`** (**CRITICAL!** If `START WITH` is omitted on a descending sequence, `START WITH` defaults to **`maxvalue`**!) |
| **Default `CACHE` / `CYCLE`** | `CACHE 1` (no cache), `NO CYCLE` | `CACHE 1`, `NO CYCLE` |

#### Why Ch.05 p. 447 Quiz Q3 Answer is **BD**!
*Question*: Create a decremental sequence `seq_1` starting at `400`, step `-4`, minimum `100`, cycling at minimum:
- **A. `CREATE SEQUENCE seq_1 START WITH 400 MAXVALUE 100 INCREMENT BY -4 CYCLE;`** -> **WRONG!** (`START WITH 400` cannot be greater than `MAXVALUE 100`, and `MINVALUE 100` is missing!)
- **B. `CREATE SEQUENCE seq_1 MAXVALUE 400 MINVALUE 100 INCREMENT BY -4 CYCLE;`** -> **CORRECT!** Because for a descending sequence (`INCREMENT BY -4`), when `START WITH` is omitted, **`START WITH` automatically defaults to `MAXVALUE` (`400`)**!
- **C. `CREATE SEQUENCE seq_1 START WITH 400 MINVALUE 100 INCREMENT BY -4 CYCLE;`** -> **WRONG!** Because `MAXVALUE` was omitted on a descending sequence, **`MAXVALUE` defaults to `-1`**, which fails because `START WITH 400 > MAXVALUE -1`!
- **D. `CREATE SEQUENCE seq_1 START WITH 400 MINVALUE 100 MAXVALUE 400 INCREMENT BY -4 CYCLE;`** -> **CORRECT!** Explicitly sets `START WITH 400`, `MINVALUE 100`, `MAXVALUE 400`, `INCREMENT BY -4`, and `CYCLE`.
key_takeaways: For an ascending sequence (`INCREMENT > 0`), default `MINVALUE = 1`, default `MAXVALUE = 2^63 - 1`, and default `START WITH = minvalue`.
For a descending sequence (`INCREMENT < 0`), default `MINVALUE = -2^63 - 1`, default `MAXVALUE = -1`, and default `START WITH = maxvalue`.

Therefore, for a decremental sequence starting at 400 down to 100 with step -4, you MUST specify `MAXVALUE 400` (`START WITH 400` is optional because it defaults to `MAXVALUE 400`) — making both B and D correct in Ch.05 p. 447 Quiz Q3!
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.05 p. 447 Quiz Q3): Why does `CREATE SEQUENCE seq_1 START WITH 400 MINVALUE 100 INCREMENT BY -4 CYCLE;` (Option C) FAIL with an error? Because for a negative increment, default `MAXVALUE` is `-1`, and `START (400)` cannot be greater than `MAXVALUE (-1)`! Both B and D are the official correct answers (`BD`).

EXAM TRAP: `OWNED BY table_name.column_name` automatically drops the sequence when that column or table is dropped, but it does NOT automatically increment the column on `INSERT` unless `DEFAULT nextval('seq')` is also declared on the column (Ch.05 p. 442).

lecture.title: Operators & Built-in Functions (String, Numeric, Date/Time, Pattern Matching, Geometric)
objectives: Master Logical Operators (`and`, `or`, `not` — Ch.05 Quiz Q3: ABC!) and the 3 Pattern Matching approaches (`LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, `POSIX regular expressions` — Ch.05 Quiz Q4: ACD!)

Evaluate Character Functions (`instr`, `overlay`, `insert`, `substring`, `replace`, `lpad`/`rpad`), Arithmetic Operators (`!!`, `@`, `|/`, `||/`, `^`, `&`, `#`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) & Functions (`sin`, `round`, `bitand`, `ceil`, `floor` — Ch.05 Quiz Q2: BC!)
Compute Date/Time Arithmetic (`SELECT date '2021-4-28' + integer '7'` — Ch.05 Quiz Q1!), Type Conversions (`cast`, `to_char`, `to_date`, `to_number`), and Geometric Operators/Functions
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Logical Operators, Pattern Matching & Character Functions (pp. 449–454, 469)
- **Logical Operators (Ch.05 p. 469 Quiz Q3: ABC!)**:
  - **`and`**, **`or`**, and **`not`** (Priority: `NOT` > `AND` > `OR`). *(`not or` is NOT a logical operator!)*
- **Three Separate Approaches to Pattern Matching (Ch.05 p. 469 Quiz Q4: ACD!)**:
  1. **`LIKE`** (traditional SQL wildcard matching with `%` and `_`).
  2. **`SIMILAR TO`** (SQL:1999 regular expressions).
  3. **`POSIX regular expressions`** (`~`, `~*`, `!~`, `!~*`). *(Option B `Same` is NOT a pattern matching method!)*
- **High-Yield Character Processing Functions (pp. 451–454)**:
  - **`instr(str1, str2, pos, nth)`**: Searches `str1` starting at `pos` for the `nth` occurrence of `str2` and returns the 1-based character index from the start of `str1` (or `0` if not found).
    - Example: `SELECT instr('abcdabcdabcd', 'bcd', 2, 2);` -> Starts at pos 2 (`'bcdabcdabcd'`), 1st match is at pos 2, **2nd match is at pos `6`**!
  - **`overlay(str PLACING newstr FROM pos [FOR len])`**: Replaces `len` chars starting at `pos`.
    - Example: `SELECT overlay('hello' PLACING 'world' FROM 2 FOR 3);` -> Replaces `'ell'` with `'world'` -> **`'hworldo'`**.
  - **`insert(str, pos, len, newstr)`**: `insert('quadratic', 5, 2, 'what')` \\equiv `replace('quadratic', 'ra', 'what')` -> `'quadwhattic'`.
  - **`substring('Thomas' FROM 2 FOR 3)`** -> **`'hom'`**; **`replace('abcdefabcdef', 'cd', 'XXX')`** -> **`'abXXXefabXXXef'`**.
  - **`lpad('hi', 5, 'xyza')`** -> **`'xyzhi'`**; **`rpad('hi', 5, 'xy')`** -> **`'hixyx'`**; **`reverse('abcde')`** -> **`'edcba'`**.
  - **`char_length('hello')`** (char count) vs. **`lengthb('hello')`** (byte count); **`ascii(str)`**; **`concat`** / **`concat_ws`** (max 8000 bytes).

---

### 2. Arithmetic Operators & Functions (pp. 455–458, 468)
- **Special Arithmetic & Bitwise Operators (p. 455)**:
  - **`!!`**: Factorial (prefix); **`@`**: Absolute value (`@ -5.0` = `5.0`); **`|/`**: Square root (`|/ 25.0` = `5`); **`||/`**: Cubic root; **`^`**: Power (`2.0^3.0` = `8.0`); **`|`**: Bitwise OR; **`&`**: Bitwise AND (`91 & 15` = `11`); **`#`**: Bitwise XOR (`17 # 5` = `20`); **`~`**: Bitwise NOT; **`<<` / `>>`**: Left/Right shift (`1 << 4` = `16`).
  - *Priority*: Four arithmetic ops (`* / % + -`) > Shift (`<< >>`) > Bitwise AND (`&`) > Bitwise XOR (`#`) > Bitwise OR (`|`).
  - *Decimal rounding difference*: Bitwise operators (`&`, `|`, `#`) **round off** decimal inputs first, whereas functions **`BITAND`**, **`BITOR`**, **`BITXOR`** **truncate (round down)** decimal inputs first!
- **Arithmetic Functions (pp. 456–458, Ch.05 p. 468 Quiz Q2: BC!)**:
  - **`sin(n)`**, **`cos(n)`**, **`acos(n)`**, **`asin(n)`**, **`abs(n)`**.
  - **`round(number [, decimals])`**: `round(1234.5678, -2)` -> **`1200`**; `round(1234.5678, 2)` -> **`1234.57`**.
  - **`bitand(29, 15)`** -> **`13`** (11101_2 \land 01111_2 = 01101_2 = 13).
  - **`ceil(-42.8)`** -> **`-42`** (smallest integer \≥ x); **`floor(-42.8)`** -> **`-43`** (largest integer \≤ x); **`trunc(42.8)`** -> **`42`**; **`div(9,4)`** -> **`2`**; **`mod(9,4)`** -> **`1`**; **`cbrt(27.0)`** -> **`3`**; **`log(100.0)`** -> **`2`**.
  - *(Note: `length(str)` and `hex(p1)` are character/string functions, so in Ch.05 p. 468 Quiz Q2 only **`B. sin(n)`** and **`C. round(v numeric, s int)`** are arithmetic functions!)*

---

### 3. Date/Time Operators, Type Conversions & Geometric Operators (pp. 459–468)
- **Date/Time Arithmetic (pp. 459–462, Ch.05 p. 468 Quiz Q1!)**:
  - Slide 106 (p. 459): `SELECT date '2021-5-28' + integer '7' AS RESULT;` outputs **`2021-06-04 00:00:00`** in openGauss (where `DATE` in A-compatibility mode includes `00:00:00` time).
  - **Ch.05 p. 468 Quiz Q1**: `SELECT date '2021-4-28' + integer '7' AS RESULT;` -> Adding 7 days to April 28 (April has 30 days) yields **May 5 (`2021-05-05` / `2021-05-05 00:00:00`)**! *(Note: The official slide 115 answer key prints `A` [`2021-05-05`], while openGauss `gsql` in default Oracle compatibility mode prints `2021-05-05 00:00:00` [Option C]. Know both why April 28 + 7 days = May 5 and the slide key `A` / runtime `C`!)*
  - **`justify_days(interval '35 days')`** -> **`1 mon 5 days`** (30-day month); **`last_day(...)`** -> last day of month.
- **Type Conversions**: `cast(x AS y)`, `to_char`, `to_clob`, `to_date`, `to_number`, `to_timestamp`, `to_bigint`, `hextoraw`, `rawtohex`, `numtoday`.
- **Geometric Operators & Functions (pp. 465–467)**:
  - Operators: `+` / `-` (translation), `*` / `/` (scaling/rotation), **`#`** (intersection), **`@-@`** (length/circumference), **`@@`** (center), **`<->`** (distance), **`&&`** (overlaps), **`<<` / `>>`** (strictly left/right of), **`<^` / `>^`** (below/above).
  - Functions: `area(obj)`, `center(obj)`, `diameter(circle)`, `radius(circle)`, `height(box)`, `width(box)`, `length(obj)`, `npoints(path/polygon)`, `isclosed(path)`, `isopen(path)`, `pclose(path)`, `popen(path)`.
key_takeaways: The arithmetic functions in Ch.05 Quiz Q2 are `B. sin(n)` and `C. round(v numeric, s int)` (`BC`); the logical operators in Quiz Q3 are `and`, `or`, `not` (`ABC`); the 3 pattern matching approaches in Quiz Q4 are `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, and `POSIX regular expressions` (`ACD`).
`instr('abcdabcdabcd', 'bcd', 2, 2)` returns `6`; `overlay('hello' placing 'world' from 2 for 3)` returns `'hworldo'`; `round(1234.5678, -2)` returns `1200`; `bitand(29, 15)` returns `13`.

`SELECT date '2021-4-28' + integer '7' AS RESULT;` adds 7 days to April 28 (30-day month) to produce May 5 (`2021-05-05` in the Ch.05 slide answer key A, or `2021-05-05 00:00:00` in openGauss A-mode runtime C).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.05 p. 469 Quiz Q4): 'Which three separate approaches to pattern matching are provided by a database?' -> `A. LIKE`, `C. SIMILAR TO`, `D. POSIX regular expressions` (`ACD`). `B. Same` does not exist!

EXAM TRAP: Watch negative numbers in `ceil(-42.8)` (`-42`, notsmaller integer) vs. `floor(-42.8)` (`-43`, not larger integer) vs. `round(1234.5678, -2)` (`1200`, rounds two digits to the left of the decimal point)!

lecture.title: GaussDB Positioning, Full-Stack Architecture & High-Availability Topologies
objectives: Contrast openGauss (open-source standalone & primary/standby) with GaussDB (commercial cloud-native distributed & centralized HTAP database)
Memorize GaussDB scale specifications (> 1,000 nodes scale-out, 4 PB storage, up to 256 shards/DNs, > 100,000 cluster concurrent connections)
Compare GaussDB deployment topologies: Centralized 1+1 vs 1+2, Intra-City Active-Active, Intra-City 3-AZ Multi-Active, 3DC Geo-Redundant, and Dual-Cluster Remote DR
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. GaussDB Positioning & Differences from openGauss (pp. 478–480)
**GaussDB** is Huawei's commercial enterprise-level distributed relational database based on the openGauss ecosystem and full-stack Kunpeng hardware/software co-design:

| Dimension | openGauss | GaussDB |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Delivery Model** | **Open-source** software (Mulan PSL v2) | **Commercial enterprise database / Cloud service** |
| **Architecture** | **Standalone** & **Primary/Standby** (1P + up to 8S) | **Distributed (Shared-Nothing MPP)** & **Centralized (Primary/Standby)** |
| **Scale & Capacity** | Single-node up to 10,000 concurrent connections; 32 TB/table | Scale-out of **> 1,000 nodes** (up to **256 shards/DNs** per large cluster), **4 PB** storage, **> 100,000 concurrent connections** per cluster (10,000 per node) |
| **Workload Focus** | Enterprise OLTP & HTAP on single cluster | Massive distributed transaction expansion + HTAP across regions/AZs |

---

### 2. Primary/Standby Replication Modes: `1+1` vs. `1+2` (p. 481)
- **`1+1` (Maximum Availability)**:
  - Data is synchronously replicated to 1 standby node. However, **if synchronous replication fails due to network issues, it automatically degrades to asynchronous replication** (and resumes synchronous replication when the network recovers). If a switchover occurs while unsynchronized, data loss may occur.
- **`1+2` (Maximum Protection)**:
  - Data is synchronously replicated to 2 standby nodes across up to 3 AZs (5 replicas supported across multiple AZs). **Confirmation from standby is required before returning commit success to the client**, guaranteeing zero data loss (`RPO = 0`).

---

### 3. Distributed High-Availability & Disaster Recovery Topologies (pp. 482–486, 522)
1. **Centralized Cluster Across 3 AZs (p. 482)**: 1 Primary (`DN + CMS + ETCD`) in AZ 1 + 2 Standby (`DN + CMS + ETCD`) in AZ 2 and AZ 3.
2. **Distributed Cluster in Intra-City Active-Active / 3-AZ Multi-Active Mode (pp. 483–484)**:
   - Shards (`DN 1..N`), `CN`s, `GTM`s, `CMS`s, and `ETCD`s are striped across 3 AZs in the same city. Every server runs **`CMA` (Cluster Manager Agent)** and **`OMA` (Operation Manager Agent)**.
3. **Distributed Cluster in Two-Site Three-Center (3DC Geo-Redundant) Mode (p. 485, 522)**:
   - E.g., **Shanghai DC 1 (AZ 1)** + **Shanghai DC 2 (AZ 2)** in intra-city active-active mode + **Beijing Remote DC (AZ 3)**. Single cluster across AZs achieves **`RPO = 0, RTO < 60s`**.
4. **Dual-Cluster Remote DR (via OBS Log Synchronization, p. 486)**:
   - Primary Cluster (AZ 1 + AZ 2 intra-city active-active) ships incremental logs via **OBS** to a remote DR Cluster (AZ 3) for physical log replay.
   - **Specifications**: **`RPO = 10 seconds`**, **`RTO = 10 minutes`**.

key_takeaways: openGauss is open-source (standalone and primary/standby), whereas GaussDB is Huawei's commercial enterprise cloud database supporting both centralized and distributed (Shared-Nothing) deployment up to >1,000 nodes (256 shards), 4 PB data, and >100,000 concurrent connections.
In Primary/Standby deployment, `1+1` is Maximum Availability (falls back to async on network fault) and `1+2` is Maximum Protection (strict sync confirmation).
In Dual-Cluster Remote DR via OBS log synchronization, the specifications are RPO = 10 seconds and RTO = 10 minutes (whereas intra-city active-active / 3DC achieves RPO = 0, RTO < 60s).
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: In GaussDB, what is the difference between `1+1` and `1+2` primary/standby modes? `1+1` is 'Maximum Availability' (switches to async replication on network fault), while `1+2` is 'Maximum Protection' (requires standby confirmation before returning to client, Ch.06 p. 481).

EXAM TRAP: In an ETCD cluster within GaussDB, there must be **3 or more ETCD instances** and the total number of ETCDs **must be an odd number** (using the Raft consensus algorithm with Leader and Follower roles, Ch.06 p. 482).

lecture.title: GaussDB Distributed Components — CN, DN, GTM, CMS & ETCD
objectives: Memorize the exact role of every GaussDB distributed component: CN, DN, GTM, CM/CMS/CMA, OM/OMA, ETCD, WLM, GDS Loader, and Storage (Ch.06 Quiz Q1: D!)
Trace the 5-step distributed parallel SQL execution flow across CNs and DNs

lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. GaussDB Distributed Architecture Components (pp. 487, 495, Ch.06 Quiz Q1!)

| Component | Full Name | Official Responsibility in GaussDB (p. 495) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`CN`** | **Coordinator Node** | Receives SQL access requests from applications, uses the optimizer to **generate distributed execution plans**, breaks down tasks and distributes fragments to DNs for parallel processing, and **summarizes/returns final results** to the client. |
| **`DN`** | **Data Node** | Stores service data (in row, column, or hybrid mode), executes data query tasks assigned by CNs, and returns result sets to CNs. |
| **`GTM`** | **Global Transaction Manager** | Generates and maintains globally unique transaction information: **global transaction ID (`GXID`), transaction snapshot, timestamp, and sequence**. |
| **`ETCD`** | **Editable Text Configuration Daemon** | Distributed key-value store (Raft consensus) **used for sharing configurations and discovering services (service registration and search) — Exact Ch.06 Quiz Q1: D!** |
| **`CM` (`CMS` + `CMA`)** | **Cluster Manager** | Manages and monitors the running status of functional units and physical resources across the distributed system, driving automatic failover. |
| **`OM` (`OMA`)** | **Operation Manager** | Provides management interfaces and tools for routine O&M and configuration management of the cluster. |
| **`Storage`** | **Local Storage** | Server's local storage resources used to store data permanently (Shared-Nothing architecture). |
| **`GDS Loader` & `WLM`** | **Gauss Data Service / Workload Manager** | High-speed parallel data loading direct to DNs (`GDS`) and workload resource management (`WLM`). |

> **Roles Perceived by the Management Plane (p. 495)**: **`DN`**, **`CN`**, **`GTM`**, **`ETCD`**, and **`CMS`**.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![GaussDB Distributed Components Architecture and Control/Data Planes (CM, GTM, CN, DN, ETCD, CMS) (Official Reference: p. 495)](./assets/images/p3_h8s2_distributed_components.png)
*Figure: GaussDB Distributed Components Architecture and Control/Data Planes (CM, GTM, CN, DN, ETCD, CMS) (Official Reference: p. 495)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 2. Five-Step Fully Parallel Distributed Execution Flow (p. 487)
1. **Step 1 (SQL Submission)**: The service application sends an SQL statement (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`/`DROP`) to a **CN**.
2. **Step 2 (Plan Generation & Dispatch)**: The **CN** uses its query optimizer to generate a distributed execution plan and dispatches plan fragments to the **DNs** (acquiring global snapshot/CSN from **GTM**).
3. **Step 3 (Inter-DN Stream Exchange)**: Because data is evenly distributed across DNs via consistent hashing, DNs exchange intermediate data when needed using **three types of Streams**:
   - **`Broadcast` Stream**: Broadcasts a small table's rows to all DNs.
   - **`Redistribution` Stream**: Re-hashes rows by join/group key across DNs.
   - **`Gather` Stream**: Collects results from DNs back to the CN.
4. **Step 4 (Result Return to CN)**: Each **DN** executes its fragment in multi-threaded parallel mode and returns its partial result set to the **CN**.
5. **Step 5 (Final Aggregation)**: The **CN** summarizes/merges the results and sends the final response to the service application.
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![GaussDB Distributed SQL Execution 5-Step Flow Across CN and DNs (Official Reference: p. 487)](./assets/images/p3_h8s2_distributed_exec_flow.png)
*Figure: GaussDB Distributed SQL Execution 5-Step Flow Across CN and DNs (Official Reference: p. 487)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. Additional High-Performance Engines in GaussDB (pp. 489–490)
- **High-Speed Parallel Data Loading (`GDS`)**: **CNs** only plan and deliver tasks while **DNs** directly import data in parallel (`CSV`, `TEXT`, or `FIXED` format), fully utilizing all nodes' I/O and network bandwidth.
- **LLVM Dynamic Compilation (JIT)**: Moves determination of the actual execution path from the executor phase to the **execution initialization phase**, eliminating function-call overhead and branch mispredictions on expression evaluation.
- **Adaptive Compression**: Automatically selects the optimal compression algorithm by data type (**`RLE`**, **`DELTA`**, **`BYTEPACK`/`BITPACK`**, **`LZ4`**, **`ZLIB`**, **`LOCAL DICTIONARY`**).
key_takeaways: In GaussDB's distributed architecture, `ETCD` is used for sharing configurations and service discovery (service registration and search) — exact Ch.06 Quiz Q1: D!

`CN` parses SQL, generates distributed plans, dispatches tasks to DNs, and aggregates final results; `DN` stores data and executes query fragments; `GTM` manages global transaction IDs, snapshots, timestamps, and sequences.
GaussDB provides three Stream operators to exchange data among DNs: `Broadcast`, `Gather`, and `Redistribution`.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP (Ch.06 Quiz Q1): 'In the GaussDB distributed architecture, which component is used for sharing configuration and service discovery (service registration and search)?' -> D. `ETCD`! Do not confuse `ETCD` with `GTM` (global transaction info) or `CM` (cluster status monitoring).

EXAM TRAP: During high-speed parallel data loading in GaussDB, does table data pass through the CN? No! CNs are only responsible for task planning and delivery, while DNs import data directly in parallel (Ch.06 p. 489).

lecture.title: GaussDB Enterprise Features — Distributed Storage, `GTM-Lite` & Physical/Logical Backup
objectives: Contrast GaussDB two-layer distributed storage: inter-shard (`Hash distribution` vs `Replication distribution`) and intra-shard (`Quorum multi-copy`)
Compare `GTM-Lite` (strongly consistent, lock-free CSN) vs. `GTM-Free` (eventually consistent, no central node)
Distinguish GaussDB Physical Backup (full + incremental to OBS) from Logical Backup (streaming table extract to local disk/OBS in TEXT/CSV)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Two-Layer Distributed Storage: Inter-Shard & Intra-Shard (p. 497)
GaussDB provides a **two-layer distributed storage architecture**:
1. **Layer 1 — Inter-Shard Data Distribution (Between Shards)**:
   - **Hash Distribution (`DISTRIBUTE BY HASH(col)`)**: Applied to **large user tables**. Hashes one or more user-specified distribution keys to spread rows evenly across shards, expanding total capacity and enabling parallel query processing and shard pruning.
   - **Replication Distribution (`DISTRIBUTE BY REPLICATION`)**: Applied to **small dimension/lookup tables**. Stores a complete copy of the table on **every shard**, allowing multi-table joins to execute locally on each DN without cross-node data redistribution!
2. **Layer 2 — Intra-Shard Data Storage (Within Each Shard)**:
   - Uses **quorum-based distributed multi-copy storage** (Primary DN + Standby DNs per shard) with automatic primary/standby switchover, AZ switchover, and forcible promotion to primary.

---

### 2. Distributed Transaction Processing: `GTM-Lite` vs. `GTM-Free` (p. 500)
Traditional distributed databases maintain a global active transaction list on the GTM, which becomes a central bottleneck. Huawei's **`GTM-Lite`** eliminates this bottleneck via three innovations:
1. **CSN Replaces Transaction Lists**: Uses a 64-bit **Commit Sequence Number (`CSN`)** to determine tuple visibility immediately without traversing a global active transaction list.
2. **Lock-Free Atomic Operations**: Assigns CSNs via lock-free atomic instructions so concurrent transactions obtain CSNs simultaneously without single-point contention.
3. **Minimal Network Overhead**: Only a single CSN integer is exchanged during node interactions.

| Transaction Mode | Consistency Level | Central GTM Dependency & Target Scenario |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`GTM-Lite` Mode** | **Strong Global Consistency** | Connects to lightweight GTM for lock-free CSN snapshots; ideal for general enterprise OLTP requiring real-time cross-shard read consistency. |
| **`GTM-Free` Mode** | **Eventual Consistency** (does not provide real-time cross-node read consistency) | **Does NOT connect to GTM** (zero central node involvement); achieves maximum throughput in **perfectly sharded OLTP scenarios**. |
<!-- PDF_FIGS_START -->
![GTM-Lite Lockless Transaction Timestamp Coordination (Official Reference: p. 500)](./assets/images/p3_h8s3_gtm_lite.png)
*Figure: GTM-Lite Lockless Transaction Timestamp Coordination (Official Reference: p. 500)*
<!-- PDF_FIGS_END -->


---

### 3. Distributed Physical Backup vs. Logical Backup (pp. 502–503)
- **Physical Backup (p. 502)**:
  - Backs up data files of each DN across the **entire cluster in parallel to OBS (Object Storage Service)** in internal database format and restores to **homogeneous databases** (supports compression, flow control, and resumable backup).
  - **Full Backup vs. Incremental Backup**:
    - **Full backup**: Backs up all data at a time point (duration proportional to total DB size).
    - **Incremental backup**: Backs up only data modified since the last backup (duration proportional to changed data size). **Restoring a complete database requires BOTH the full backup and subsequent incremental backups** (e.g., Monday Full + Tue–Sun Incrementals).
- **Logical Backup (p. 503)**:
  - Extracts user table records from each DN in parallel streaming mode to **local disk files or OBS in `TEXT` or `CSV` format**, and can restore data into **homogeneous OR heterogeneous databases**.
key_takeaways: Between shards, GaussDB uses Hash distribution for large tables and Replication distribution (a full copy on every shard) for small lookup tables to accelerate multi-table joins.

`GTM-Lite` provides strong global consistency using lock-free CSNs (replacing active transaction lists), whereas `GTM-Free` provides eventual consistency without connecting to GTM for perfectly sharded OLTP.

Physical backup writes internal-format cluster files to OBS for homogeneous restore (Full + Incremental), whereas Logical backup streams user tables in TEXT/CSV to local disk or OBS for homogeneous or heterogeneous restore.
exam_traps: EXAM TRAP: Can you restore a complete database using ONLY an incremental physical backup? No! A complete database can be restored only when BOTH the full backup and incremental backups are used together (Ch.06 p. 502).
EXAM TRAP: Do not confuse `GTM-Lite` (strongly consistent, uses lock-free CSNs) with `GTM-Free` (eventually consistent, does not connect to GTM).

Contrast DAS (Standard, Cloud DBA, Enterprise DevOps), DRS (Real-time migration, Backup migration, Real-time synchronization, Data subscription, Real-time DR), and UGO (heterogeneous schema/SQL migration)
Identify Huawei Cloud security/monitoring services: CTS (7-day console trace query + OBS/KMS dump), CES (resource/log monitoring), and DBSS (bypass security audit + DB firewall)
lecture.content_markdown:
### 1. Database Management, Replication & Migration Suite: `DAS`, `DRS`, `UGO` (pp. 505–512)

#### A. `DAS` (Data Admin Service, p. 505)
One-stop web-based cloud database management console with **3 editions**:
1. **Standard Edition (for Developers)**: Web client, online SQL editing, intelligent SQL prompts without local client installation.
2. **Cloud DBA (for DBAs & O&M)**: Instance performance metrics, slow SQL analysis, SQL explorer, real-time and historical diagnosis.
3. **Enterprise Edition (for Enterprise DevOps)**: Automatic identification of modification risks + permission approval workflows to ensure secure data changes.

#### B. `DRS` (Data Replication Service, pp. 506–509)
Cloud service for **real-time database data migration and synchronization** offering **5 functions**: *Real-time migration*, *Backup migration*, *Real-time synchronization*, *Data subscription*, and *Real-time DR*:
- **Real-Time Migration**: Online incremental data migration across public networks, VPCs, VPNs, or Direct Connect with minimal downtime.
- **Backup Migration**: Exports source DB backup files -> uploads to **OBS** -> DRS downloads and restores to destination DB **without exposing the source DB's IP address or connecting directly** (currently supports migrating **SQL Server** to the cloud, p. 508).
- **Real-Time Synchronization**: Continuous real-time data flow (many-to-one, one-to-many, different table names) for real-time analytics, reporting, and data warehouses.

#### C. `UGO` (Database and Application Migration UGO, pp. 510–512, Ch.06 Quiz Q2!)
Professional tool focused on **heterogeneous database object/schema migration and application SQL migration** (e.g., from Oracle 10g/11g/12c, DB2, Teradata, SQL Server to GaussDB / RDS).
- **The 6 Official Core Functions of UGO (Slide 37, p. 512 & Ch.06 Quiz Q2 Answer!)**:
  1. **Source database profiling**
  2. **Destination database selection and specification recommendation**
  3. **Destination database compatibility analysis**
  4. **Migration workload evaluation**
  5. **Database structure migration**
  6. **Application SQL migration**

### 2. Cloud Security & Monitoring Services: `CTS`, `CES`, `DBSS` (pp. 513–520)

| Service | Full Name | Core Capabilities & Exam Specifications |

| **`CTS`** | **Cloud Trace Service** | Log audit service recording console/API operations on cloud resources. **Console queries cover the last 7 days**; dumps compressed trace files to **OBS** for long-term storage encrypted via **KMS**. |
| **`CES`** | **Cloud Eye Service** | Resource & database monitoring platform (automatic/server monitoring, real-time alarm notifications, OBS dumping, resource grouping, error/slow log & trace monitoring). |
| **`DBSS`** | **Database Security Service** | Includes **Database Protection (DB firewall, data breach prevention)** and **Database Security Audit**. Deployed in **bypass mode**; provides user behavior detection (associating app & DB layers), multi-dimensional lead analysis (Risk, Session, Statement leads), real-time SQL injection/blacklist/whitelist alarms, and **Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX)** compliance reports. |

questions.question: (Official Ch.01 Quiz Q1) Which of the following is NOT a component of a database system (DBS)?

questions.question: (Official Ch.01 Quiz Q2) Which of the following statements about the ACID feature of database transactions is INCORRECT?
options: A. A indicates atomicity, whereby operations in a transaction are either all successful or all failed.
B. C refers to consistency, whereby the system status can only be the status before the transaction or after the transaction is successful. No inconsistent intermediate status can occur.

C. I refers to availability, whereby the database system must provide the highest availability possible for transaction execution in order to ensure as many successfully executed transactions as possible.
D. D refers to durability, whereby the status of a successful transaction can be maintained, even if the machine is powered off.
questions.explanation: Per Chapter 01 (p. 22 & p. 67), 'I' in ACID stands for Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere with one another), NOT Availability.

questions.question: According to the openGauss technical specifications (Ch.01 p. 57), what is the maximum number of partitions supported in a single partitioned table for Range partitioning versus Hash/List partitioning?
questions.explanation: Per Chapter 01 (p. 57), a partitioned table in openGauss supports up to 32,768 partitions for range partitioning and 64 partitions for hash or list partitioning.

questions.question: (Official Ch.02 Quiz Q1) Which of the following is NOT an openGauss server tool?

questions.question: (Official Ch.02 Quiz Q2) When the `gs_checkperf` tool is used to check system performance, which of the following can be viewed ONLY by user `root`?
